articles.title: "What If Your CSS Compiler Could Catch Accessibility Bugs Before Production?"
articles.description: Modern frontend development has become increasingly sophisticated.  We have component-driven...
articles.body_html:
Modern frontend development has become increasingly sophisticated.

We have component-driven architectures, server components, powerful build tools, automated testing, design systems, and AI coding assistants.

Yet one problem remains surprisingly common:

We still discover many styling and accessibility problems too late.

A color combination fails contrast requirements. A component introduces duplicated CSS. A dark theme needs additional overrides. An RTL layout breaks because physical spacing properties were used. A styling engine adds work to the browser that could have been completed during the build.

What if your styling system could prevent these problems before your application ships?

That is the idea behind "traceless-style" (https://traceless-style.dev/).

It is an open-source, MIT-licensed, build-time atomic CSS library designed around three principles:

  • Zero-runtime styling for compiled style declarations.
  • Automated accessibility validation.
  • Intelligent styling diagnostics and transformations.

Let's explore what this approach looks like in practice.

  1. Move CSS work from runtime to build time

Traditional runtime CSS-in-JS approaches can involve generating class names, processing styles, maintaining caches, or inserting CSS rules while an application runs.

These operations are not necessarily expensive in every application, but they introduce work that may be avoidable.

traceless-style takes a different approach.

Instead of processing compiled styles in the browser, it transforms "tl.create()" calls during the build process into ordinary class-name strings.

For example:

import { tl } from "traceless-style";

const $ = tl.create({
card: {
padding: "1.5rem",
background: "#ffffff",
color: "#0f172a",
borderRadius: "12px",

_hover: {
  transform: "translateY(-2px)",
},

_dark: {
  background: "#13131a",
},

},
});

export function Card() {
return (


Build faster. Ship cleaner.

);
}

During compilation, the styling declaration is transformed into generated class names, while the corresponding atomic CSS rules are emitted into a static stylesheet.

The result:

  • No runtime styling engine for transformed declarations.
  • No runtime style injection for compiled styles.
  • Reusable atomic CSS rules.
  • Automatic deduplication of identical property-value combinations.
  • A stylesheet generated before production deployment.

The browser receives the compiled output rather than having to interpret the original styling object.

The central idea is simple: do the styling work before the user visits the application.

Technical explanation:
https://traceless-style.dev/docs/learn/01-introduction

  1. Accessibility should be part of the build process

This is where the project takes an interesting direction.

Accessibility is often handled through manual reviews, separate testing tools, or checks performed late in development.

But color contrast problems can be introduced by something as simple as changing a text color or background.

traceless-style includes build-time contrast validation based on WCAG requirements.

It checks relevant contrast requirements, including:

  • WCAG AA: 4.5:1 for normal text.
  • WCAG AAA: 7:1 for normal text.
  • UI component contrast requirements.
  • Focus-indicator contrast requirements.

It also provides APCA Lc readings as an additional perception-oriented measurement.

Consider this diagnostic example:

traceless-style build

✘ TLS0301 app/Button.tsx:24:7

WCAG 2.1 §1.4.3
AA 4.5:1 not met.

Foreground: #94a3b8
Background: #ffffff

Contrast ratio: 2.85:1

Suggested replacement: #475569
Contrast ratio: 7.55:1

Run with --fix-contrast to apply.

Instead of discovering the issue after deployment, developers can receive actionable feedback during the build process.

The interactive contrast-fixing workflow can also suggest alternative colors.

This changes the role of accessibility from a final checklist into part of the development workflow.

Important: automated contrast checks do not replace complete accessibility testing, keyboard testing, screen-reader testing, or evaluation with real users.

Documentation:
https://traceless-style.dev/docs

  1. Automatic dark mode without duplicating every color

Dark mode is easy to demonstrate and surprisingly easy to implement inconsistently.

A typical application may contain hundreds of components, each with different backgrounds, text colors, borders, and interactive states.

Maintaining all those variations manually can become difficult.

traceless-style can derive dark variants for colors during compilation, while allowing explicit overrides when necessary.

For example:

const $ = tl.create({
panel: {
background: "#ffffff",
color: "#0f172a",
borderRadius: "12px",

_dark: {
  background: "#13131a",
},

},
});

You can retain control over individual dark-mode decisions without manually duplicating every declaration.

The goal is to make theme support part of the styling architecture rather than a separate layer of repetitive CSS.

  1. RTL support built into the styling workflow

Global applications need more than English interfaces.

Arabic, Hebrew, Persian, and other right-to-left languages introduce additional layout requirements.

Developers frequently encounter problems when using physical CSS properties such as:

margin-left: 16px;
padding-right: 12px;

A layout designed around physical directions can become difficult to maintain across LTR and RTL interfaces.

traceless-style supports automatic RTL transformations by rewriting physical properties into logical CSS equivalents during compilation.

For example, a left-side margin can be transformed into its logical inline-start equivalent.

This is particularly useful for teams building multilingual applications and shared design systems.

One styling architecture can serve different writing directions without requiring developers to maintain separate copies of every component.

  1. Atomic CSS and stylesheet deduplication

Large applications often contain repeated styling declarations across many components.

Atomic CSS addresses this by representing individual CSS property-value combinations as reusable classes.

Imagine hundreds of components using:

display: flex;

Rather than repeatedly emitting identical declarations, the compiler can reuse the corresponding generated atomic rule.

traceless-style also provides:

  • "tl.defineTokens()" for design tokens.
  • "tl.createTheme()" for theme creation.
  • "tl.merge()" for style composition.
  • "tl.cx()" for class composition.
  • "tl.extend()" for reusable style extensions.
  • "tl.keyframes()" for animations.

This creates a more structured styling environment as an application grows.

  1. More than a CSS library: a developer tooling ecosystem

A modern developer tool should fit into the workflow developers already use.

The traceless-style ecosystem includes:

Compiler

Transforms styling declarations into generated atomic CSS during the build.

CLI

Provides commands for initialization, extraction, development, production builds, auditing, and inspection.

VS Code extension

Provides features including autocomplete, color swatches, hover documentation, and inline diagnostics.

Browser DevTools extension

Helps inspect generated styling classes in the browser.

Framework integrations

Supports environments including:

  • Next.js
  • Vite
  • Remix
  • Astro
  • SvelteKit
  • Qwik
  • Solid
  • Webpack
  • Rollup
  • esbuild

The objective is not simply to introduce another way to write CSS.

It is to create a connected workflow covering styling, compilation, validation, and debugging.

  1. Install it and try it in a real project

You can install traceless-style using npm:

npm install traceless-style

Or pnpm:

pnpm add traceless-style

Then initialize your project:

npx traceless-style init

Start the development workflow:

npx traceless-style dev

For production:

npx traceless-style build

You can also run the contrast-fixing workflow:

npx traceless-style --fix-contrast

The initialization command detects supported project frameworks and helps configure the integration.

No complicated setup process is required for the standard supported configurations.

Start with a small component, inspect the generated CSS, and evaluate the workflow in your own project.

  1. Why this approach matters as AI-assisted development grows

AI coding tools are changing how frontend applications are created.

Developers can now generate components, layouts, themes, and entire application interfaces much faster than before.

But generating code is not the same as generating reliable production-ready code.

AI-generated interfaces can still contain:

  • Poor color contrast.
  • Inconsistent design tokens.
  • Duplicated styling declarations.
  • Incorrect RTL behavior.
  • Unnecessary runtime styling work.

A build-time styling system with automated validation offers another layer of engineering discipline.

Instead of relying entirely on developers or AI assistants to remember every styling rule, the compiler can enforce defined constraints.

This is an interesting direction for the future of frontend infrastructure.

  1. Open source and developer contributions

traceless-style is released under the MIT license.

Developers can explore the implementation, evaluate its architecture, use it in their projects, and contribute improvements.

The project is actively documented through its official documentation and source repository.

Useful resources:

  • Official website: https://traceless-style.dev/
  • Documentation: https://traceless-style.dev/docs
  • Installation guide: https://traceless-style.dev/docs/learn/02-installation
  • npm package: https://www.npmjs.com/package/traceless-style
  • GitHub repository: https://github.com/sparkgoldentech/traceless-style
  • VS Code extension: https://marketplace.visualstudio.com/items?itemName=SparkGoldenTech.traceless-style-vscode
  1. Let's discuss the future of CSS tooling

I would love to hear from frontend engineers, open-source maintainers, and developers working on large applications.

A few questions:

  1. Do you prefer build-time CSS compilation over runtime CSS-in-JS?
  2. Should accessibility validation be a mandatory part of every production build?
  3. Would automatic dark-mode and RTL transformations simplify your design system?
  4. How should CSS tooling evolve to support AI-generated interfaces?
  5. What would you improve in a zero-runtime styling architecture?

If you are interested in modern CSS architecture, frontend performance, accessibility engineering, or developer tooling, give traceless-style a try.

Install it. Test it against a real component. Inspect the generated output. Share your feedback.

Explore the project:

https://traceless-style.dev/

GitHub:
https://github.com/sparkgoldentech/traceless-style

npm:
https://www.npmjs.com/package/traceless-style

articles.title: JavaScript noindex Removal: Fix the Initial HTML Before Trusting the DOM
articles.description: If a public page's initial HTML contains a noindex robots tag, do not rely on JavaScript to remove it...
articles.body_html:
If a public page's initial HTML contains a noindex robots tag, do not rely on JavaScript to remove it later. Fix the initial response for the pages intended to be indexed, then verify the rendered document and the route states separately. A clean browser DOM is useful evidence, but it does not erase an earlier directive in a different processing path.

For a SaaS team, this can hide a clear buyer answer behind a template mistake. The product page may describe a real capability, load normally and pass a visual review. The writer keeps improving the answer while the original response still tells a search engine to exclude it. Trace the directive before expanding the copy.

Establish the intended policy for the exact URL

Start by naming the public page and deciding whether it is supposed to be eligible for indexing. Record the full URL, including any query string relevant to the problem. Do not begin by deleting every noindex tag across the application. A public product explanation and a private account screen have different purposes, even when they share a frontend shell.

Write down the reason for the intended policy. A product guide may answer a buyer question that the company wants people to find. A temporary internal preview may intentionally stay out of search. That distinction belongs in the diagnosis, so a developer does not “repair” a deliberate publishing choice while trying to help marketing.

Keep access protection separate from this editorial policy. Removing an indexing directive is not a reason to publish private content or weaken authentication. Work on a public, approved page and preserve the existing protection around other routes. If the intended audience is unclear, resolve that specific question with the page owner before changing the response.

Inspect the initial HTML before the rendered head

Google's JavaScript SEO documentation warns that encountering noindex may cause Google to skip rendering and JavaScript execution. Removing or changing that tag with JavaScript may therefore fail to have the intended effect. Google advises against putting noindex in the original code when the page should be indexed.

Use that documented behavior to choose the first diagnostic step. Capture the response for the exact public URL using your normal development tools. Search the returned HTML for robots directives and retain the relevant portion of the head. Record the response conditions and release version alongside the finding so another developer can reproduce it.

Then inspect the rendered head in a fresh browser load. Compare what arrived with what the application eventually produced. If the initial response says noindex and the later document does not, that difference is the issue to investigate. Avoid calling the later DOM the “real page” in a way that makes the earlier response disappear from the evidence.

Trace which layer supplied the directive

A fictional product, Fieldglass Notes, uses one application shell for public guides and account pages. Its public guide about approval history receives a default noindex tag. After the page loads, a component removes the tag for public content. This is a hypothetical failure pattern, not an observed behavior of a real service.

The fix begins with ownership. Ask which part of the publishing path creates the initial head: a template, a route-specific server response, a static export or another documented layer in that application. Follow the actual output back to its source. Do not assume the page component that removes the tag also owns the response that added it.

Propose a narrow change: public guide URLs receive their intended initial indexing policy, while account and preview routes keep theirs. Review a representative URL from each affected class. The important regression question is not merely whether one guide lost noindex. It is whether the implementation now applies the right policy to each type of page it serves.

Verify direct loads and client-side navigation

Test a direct request to the repaired URL. Start a new browser context or use the team's established method for checking an uncached public response. Confirm that the initial HTML carries the intended policy, then inspect the resulting rendered head. Save both observations against the same release so the evidence describes one implementation.

Next, navigate to the guide through the application. Check the final URL and head after moving between pages with different policies. A direct load and an in-app transition are separate test cases. This is a recommended regression check for applications with changing route state, not a claim that every framework has the same metadata behavior.

For Fieldglass Notes, use the public guide, a public error route and a protected account route as clearly separate cases. Do not log private account content into a public SEO report. The developer can record whether the expected policy remained in place without copying confidential page text. Keep the test evidence proportional to the actual defect being investigated.

Check error states without turning every failure into an answer

A public page should not become an indexable empty shell merely because the initial tag was removed. Examine what the application displays when its content request fails or the requested item does not exist. Record how those states are intended to behave and compare the response and rendered output with that policy.

Google's JavaScript guide includes approaches to handling client-side error pages. Follow the parts relevant to the site's actual implementation rather than copying an isolated example into every route. In particular, distinguish a real missing resource from a temporary data-fetch problem. The right implementation depends on what the page can truthfully return under those conditions.

The editorial check is straightforward: can a reader reach the promised public answer on a normal load? If the answer disappears after a content request, a correct robots directive alone has not completed the task. Give the content availability problem its own ticket and evidence. Do not hide it under a general label such as “Google has trouble with JavaScript.”

Verify the saved buyer answer after the repair

Return to the passage that made the page worth discovering. For the fictional approval-history guide, that might explain which events are retained and who can view them. Check that the actual public page still contains the answer and its qualifiers. A technical repair should preserve the useful explanation rather than replacing it with a thin diagnostic placeholder.

Use the relevant native inspection tools to examine the repaired public output. Record which view was checked, the URL, the date and the specific directive or passage observed. A successful rendering observation is evidence about that test. It should not be reported as a guarantee of indexing, ranking or a citation in an AI-generated answer.

Keep engine-specific claims bounded. This article's warning about initial noindex comes from Google's documentation. Do not assume Claude, ChatGPT or every other retrieval system processes the same response in the same way. If the business question concerns another surface, use its current guidance and collect observations there as a separate investigation.

Leave a handoff that prevents the same mistake

The completion note should name the original response, the source of its directive and the narrow change made. Include the affected route classes and the cases checked after the repair. “Fixed SEO metadata” hides too much. “Public guide responses no longer inherit the account-shell noindex default” describes a reviewable outcome for this hypothetical application.

Add one meaningful regression check at the layer that introduced the problem. Its purpose is to catch an unintended initial directive on a public route while preserving the intended policy elsewhere. Avoid a large suite of tests that simply repeats the implementation line by line. The useful test fails when the public/private policy boundary is crossed again.

Finally, return the discovery question to the content team with honest limits. The initial HTML and rendered document have been checked for the intended policy; later indexing and AI visibility remain outcomes to observe. That handoff lets writers improve buyer answers for a clear reason, while developers can show that the public delivery path is no longer contradicting the page's purpose.

articles.title: Sistemas de Recomendação em Produção com LSH Forest, MinHash e Cache LRU Serverless (latência de 200ms)
articles.description: Quando falamos de Inteligência Artificial hoje, quase toda a atenção vai para LLMs. Mas em produtos...
articles.body_html:
Quando falamos de Inteligência Artificial hoje, quase toda a atenção vai para LLMs. Mas em produtos de alto volume — como e-commerce, delivery e plataformas de saúde — Sistemas de Recomendação Clássicos continuam sendo a espinha dorsal da personalização em larga escala.

Durante 12 meses de pesquisa e extensão na Universidade Estadual de Feira de Santana (UEFS), sob orientação do Prof. Dr. João Batista da Rocha Junior, projetei e coloquei em produção o módulo de recomendação do LogicFarma (plataforma SaaS da Farmácia Universitária com mais de 4.700 operações registradas, 666 históricos clínicos avaliados e 1.060 medicamentos).

O desafio de engenharia era claro: como recomendar procedimentos e consultas personalizadas para centenas de pacientes em tempo real e em disparos em lote (e-mail/WhatsApp), rodando sobre funções Serverless com limites rígidos de memória e tempo de execução?

Neste artigo, compartilho a arquitetura Memory-First, a adaptação do Locality-Sensitive Hashing (LSH Forest) com MinHash e a estratégia de degradação graciosa em 4 níveis que levou a latência de consulta para ~200ms.

1. O gargalo da Filtragem Colaborativa tradicional O(N × M)

Na Filtragem Colaborativa Baseada no Usuário, queremos encontrar pacientes com histórico clínico semelhante ao paciente-alvo e recomendar procedimentos que esses vizinhos realizaram, mas que o paciente ainda não conhece.

A métrica natural para conjuntos binários (realizou / não realizou um procedimento) é a Similaridade de Jaccard:

J(A, B) = |A ∩ B| / |A ∪ B|

O problema é que comparar um paciente contra todos os outros a cada requisição tem custo linear no número de usuários e itens. Em um endpoint HTTP ou num disparo de mensagens para 300 pacientes de uma vez, calcular Jaccard exato no banco de dados é inviável.

2. MinHash + LSH Forest: busca aproximada em tempo sublinear

Baseado nos experimentos de Rocha-Junior et al. (2025) sobre sistemas de recomendação com LSH em e-commerce, substituímos a comparação exata por duas estruturas probabilísticas:

  1. MinHash (l = 200 permutações): transforma o conjunto de procedimentos e consultas de cada paciente (de tamanho variável) em uma assinatura compacta de comprimento fixo l = 200. A probabilidade de duas assinaturas coincidirem em uma posição é exatamente igual à Similaridade de Jaccard entre os conjuntos. Os experimentos mostraram que l = 200 atinge o pico de Precisão Média (15,1%) mantendo Recall próximo de 92%, enquanto l = 250 degrada a relação custo/precisão em RAM.
  2. LSH Forest (Bawa et al., WWW 2005): em vez do LSH tradicional (que exige calibrar manualmente o número de buckets e o limiar de similaridade), utilizamos uma floresta de árvores de prefixos auto-ajustável (MinHashLSHForest), consultando k_build = 80 vizinhos na indexação e k_query = 20 vizinhos em tempo real.

3. Adaptação do E-commerce para o Domínio Clínico

No modelo original de e-commerce, as interações possuem pesos graduados (visited = 1, cart_added = 4, bought = 8). No domínio farmacêutico, a interação é estritamente binária (o paciente realizou ou não o procedimento/consulta).

Fizemos três adaptações de domínio:

  • Unificação de pesos por co-ocorrência: cada item é codificado como "Nome|Categoria" (ex.: "Glicemia|Procedimento", "Cefaleia|Consulta"), e a pontuação dos itens candidatos nos k = 20 vizinhos mais próximos é calculada pela frequência de co-ocorrência entre os vizinhos que possuem o item (excluindo o que o paciente já realizou).
  • Filtro de elegibilidade e outliers: apenas perfis com min_items = 2 até max_items = 100 entram no índice LSH Forest.
  • Filtro determinístico por restrição clínica de gênero: consultas exclusivas ao público feminino (como "Cólica Menstrual") são filtradas tanto na saída do LSH quanto na pré-computação do ranking de fallback masculino (GLOBAL_MASCULINO).

4. Arquitetura Memory-First com Cache LRU e Batch Inference

Como a aplicação principal rodava em Next.js / TypeScript e a biblioteca de referência acadêmica para LSH (datasketch) estava em Python, separamos o motor de recomendação em funções Serverless Python integradas ao MongoDB.

Para evitar ler e desserializar o índice do banco a cada chamada, desenhamos uma arquitetura Memory-First:

[Cron Mensal Python] ---> Constrói LSH Forest (l=200) ---> Serializa blobs no MongoDB
                                                                  |
[Next.js Top Tags]   ---> POST /api/lsh/batch (até 300 pac.) ---> Cache LRU em RAM (50 farmácias)
  • Cold Start (~2 a 3s): carrega os pickle blobs (forestBlob, minhashesBlob, fallbacksBlob, itemsByPatientBlob) do MongoDB e hidrata o container.
  • Warm Start (~0,2 a 0,3s): o Cache LRU em RAM responde diretamente da memória da função Serverless, sem tocar no banco.
  • Endpoint em Lote (/api/lsh/batch): quando o farmacêutico dispara comunicados com Top Tags (#Top3ProcedimentosRec, #Top3ConsultasRec), o módulo recommendationTagResolver.ts agrupa até 300 pacientes em uma única chamada HTTP POST, carregando o cache da farmácia uma só vez.

5. Degradação Graciosa em 4 Níveis (Zero Falha no Disparo)

Em um sistema real, o algoritmo de recomendação nunca pode derrubar o fluxo principal de comunicação (seja por cold start de um paciente novo sem histórico, seja por timeout de rede). Implementamos 4 níveis de degradação:

  1. LSH Completo (lsh): os 20 vizinhos do LSH Forest preenchem todas as k sugestões pedidas.
  2. LSH Parcial + Suplementação (lsh_partial): quando os vizinhos têm pouca variedade, o sistema completa as vagas faltantes com o Fallback Global segmentado por gênero (GLOBAL_FEMININO ou GLOBAL_MASCULINO).
  3. Fallback de Cold Start (fallback): paciente recém-cadastrado (sem histórico) recebe imediatamente o ranking global segmentado pré-computado em memória, ou via leitura direta da coleção recomendacoesMensais.
  4. Fail-safe de Timeout (30s): se a API Python falhar, as Top Tags degradam para string vazia e a mensagem transacional segue normalmente.

Em produção na Farmácia Universitária da UEFS, o indexador processou 666 históricos de pacientes em 4 unidades, indexando 353 perfis elegíveis e 1.978 registros clínicos em menos de 1,7 segundo.

articles.title: Pagination Testing: Can a Peer Find the Record Beyond Page One?
articles.description: Pagination testing should show whether someone can find the right record beyond the first page and...
articles.body_html:
Pagination testing should show whether someone can find the right record beyond the first page and return to their work without losing context. A public SaaS demo that only opens page one leaves that question unanswered, even when the pagination controls look finished.

For a developer building in public, this is a useful task to share with founder peers. Give them a safe dataset, a specific record to locate and a reason to open it. Then observe where the route becomes unclear. You get a more concrete conversation than asking whether the new table looks good.

The following test plan uses a fictional invoicing product. It is a proposed workflow, not a report of testing a real product. All customer names, records and situations should be synthetic in any public version you create.

Start with a record that is not immediately visible

Create enough sample invoices to require several pages at the page size used in the demo. Put a known target somewhere beyond the first page, and record its identity in your private test notes so you can check what the peer eventually opens.

The task might be: find the unpaid invoice for a named fictional customer, open its details and return to the invoice list to continue checking overdue work. Do not tell the reviewer which page contains it. That would remove part of the navigation question.

Include plausible distractors. Two invoices might belong to the same sample customer but have different dates or payment states. The point is to see whether someone identifies the correct record, not merely whether they can operate a Next button.

Before inviting anyone, confirm that the task is possible with the supplied account and data. A reviewer should not need access to your development tools, private database or personal explanation to complete the route you are asking them to assess.

Establish what pagination is doing

The U.S. Web Design System's pagination guidance describes pagination as dividing content across pages. Its guidance also covers navigation labels, the current page and testing an implementation in its own context. Using a familiar component does not verify the surrounding product flow.

In your demo, explain what one page contains. Is the list filtered to unpaid invoices, or does it show every invoice? Does the page indicator refer to the current filtered set? Can the reviewer tell whether additional results exist?

Avoid adding implementation detail that the reviewer cannot use. They do not need a description of your database cursor to say that they expected another page of unpaid invoices. Developers can investigate the technical cause after the task exposes the confusing behavior.

If the list has a changing or unknown total, describe that honestly. Do not display a precise final page merely because a static mockup had room for one. The interface should reflect what the product actually knows about the available results.

Change the filter while away from page one

After the reviewer has moved forward, ask them to limit the list to a different payment state. Observe what happens to the current page and the visible explanation of the results.

A useful question is whether the new view makes sense on its own. If the filter leaves fewer pages than the previous view, does the product show a useful result or an unexplained empty table? If it moves to the first page, can the reviewer understand that they are viewing a new set?

Do not assume there is one correct page-reset behavior for every product. Write the intended behavior for your workflow, then compare it with the actual experience. The test should expose a mismatch between the chosen design and the task, rather than enforce a rule you never considered.

Repeat with a filter that deliberately matches no records. A legitimate empty result needs a different explanation from a failed request. Ask the peer what they think happened before you explain it. Their answer may reveal whether the state communicates the distinction.

Sort the collection, not just the visible rows

Give the reviewer a task that depends on ordering across pages, such as finding the oldest unpaid sample invoice. Then ask them to change the sort order and explain which record they expect to appear first.

Check whether the behavior matches the product's stated scope. If a control is presented as sorting the whole list, sorting only the currently loaded rows would create a misleading route through the collection. A polished arrow beside the column name would not resolve that problem.

Include records with equal values in the chosen sort field. Watch for records appearing twice or disappearing while the reviewer moves between pages. These observations are reasons to investigate ordering and page boundaries; they are not enough by themselves to diagnose a particular backend defect.

Record the relevant conditions with the observation: the selected filter, sort direction, page and target record. A report that simply says pagination is broken gives a collaborator far less to reproduce.

Open details and follow the return path

Once the reviewer finds the target, ask them to open it, inspect a safe detail and return to the list. Let them choose the return control they naturally notice. That may be a product link or the browser's Back button.

Look at what survives: the filter, sort order, page and enough position context to continue the task. The product may deliberately reset some state, but that choice should fit the work rather than happen accidentally because the list remounted.

Now ask the reviewer to locate the next invoice they intended to inspect. If they must rebuild the previous view from memory, note the extra work and ask what context they expected to keep. Avoid coaching them through the return route while claiming they completed it independently.

Check the same path after reloading the details page when that is a supported product action. A navigation flow that works only when entered from one particular demo sequence can be fragile for someone following a shared link later.

Notice keyboard access and changing data

Run a separate pass using the keyboard. Check whether the pagination controls can be reached and operated, whether their labels explain the action, and whether the current page is conveyed. Inspect your rendered implementation instead of assuming the component library guarantees the result.

Also decide what the test should do when the sample collection changes. You can add or remove a synthetic record between page visits and observe the outcome. Keep that controlled change separate from the first usability pass so you know which conditions produced the observation.

A moving collection may need different behavior from a stable report. The test's purpose is to understand the tradeoff you have implemented, including whether someone can still find a known record. It does not require promising that every list will remain identical while other users change it.

Share the task and the limits of the result

Buildside is a place for founders to share progress, questions and lessons. A public-building update about pagination can include the task, a safe demo link and one question about the route through the records.

Publish what you changed after reviewing the observations. Distinguish a peer finding the right invoice from a peer saying that the list looks clean. Both can be encouraging, but only one directly answers the retrieval question you set.

Preserve useful uncertainty. One founder completing the task does not establish that every customer, browser or access method can do so. A failed attempt may reveal an interface problem, an unsuitable task or a broken demo account. Investigate before generalizing.

Your next release note can be concrete: what navigation behavior changed, why it mattered to the task and which paths you rechecked. That gives developers and potential users a visible account of the work. Pagination becomes more than a row of controls when the public demo follows a real task all the way back to the list.

articles.description: Far away in the galaxy, there was a beautiful planet called necoz. 🌌  One day, the King of necoz...
articles.body_html:
Far away in the galaxy, there was a beautiful planet called necoz. 🌌

One day, the King of necoz announced something very exciting:

📢 Attention, everyone! Today we are hosting the biggest Cat Party in the entire galaxy! All cats are invited!

Cats from different galaxies started arriving. Some came by UFO, some came by spaceship, and one cat even arrived on a flying pizza! 🍕

🛸 Scene 1: 30 Cats and a Confused King

The party finally started.

The King looked around and shouted:

WHAT?! There are 30 cats here! Who is going to count all of them?

Suddenly, a little cat wearing sunglasses said:

Bro, just use Python!

The King opened his laptop and wrote:

cats = 30

print(cats)

Output:

30

The King: "WOW! Python counted them without even asking for their names!"

And that's how the King discovered Variables.

A variable is like a container that stores information.

In this example:

  • cats is the variable name.
  • 30 is the value.
  • = is the assignment operator.

🍕 Scene 2: 10 More Hungry Cats!

Suddenly, a UFO landed near the party.

10 more cats came out.

Their leader shouted:

WE WANT FOOD! WE ARE STARVING!

The King replied:

Bro, this is a party, not a free restaurant!

He updated his Python code:

cats = 30

cats = 40

print(cats)

Output:

40

The King: "WAIT! We had 30 cats, and now we have 40!"

That's the magic of variables. We can change the value stored in a variable.

🎂 Scene 3: The Great Cake Disaster

The King ordered 5 cakes for the party.

But one cat grabbed a cake and shouted:

THIS CAKE IS MINE!

Another cat replied:
NO! I SAW IT FIRST!

Meanwhile, a third cat(@hanzla ) was already escaping with the entire cake box. 😂

The King decided to store the information in separate variables.

cats = 40
cakes = 5

print(cats)
print(cakes)

Output:

40
5

Now Python knows that there are 40 cats and 5 cakes.

Each variable stores its own value.

😹 Scene 4: Different Types of Data

The King wanted to record more information about the party.

So he wrote:

planet = "necoz"
cats = 40
party_started = True
cake_price = 250.50

His assistant cat asked:

Why do these values look different?

The King explained:

Variable Value Data Type
planet "necoz" String
cats 40 Integer
party_started True Boolean
cake_price 250.50 Float

Let's understand them:

  • String: Stores text or words.
  • Integer: Stores whole numbers.
  • Boolean: Stores True or False.
  • Float: Stores decimal numbers.

The cat replied:

OMG! So I can also become a variable?

The King: "Yes, but please stop eating the cake!" 😂

💻 Scene 5: The Final Python Experiment

The King decided to display all the party information together.

planet = "necoz"
cats = 40
cakes = 5
party_started = True

print("Welcome to", planet)
print("Total Cats:", cats)
print("Total Cakes:", cakes)
print("Party Started:", party_started)

Output:

Welcome to necoz
Total Cats: 40
Total Cakes: 5
Party Started: True

The King shouted:

FINALLY! I AM A PYTHON DEVELOPER!

But suddenly, a cat @effessdev interrupted:
Developer later, bro. First, order 40 more cakes!

And that's how the biggest cat party in the galaxy continued all night. 🐱🎉

articles.title: How I Made a Markov Chain Model from Scratch in C++ During a Global Online Teen Hackathon
articles.description: Stardance, a global teen online hackathon hosted for teenagers by Hack Club, a nonprofit...
articles.body_html:
Stardance, a global teen online hackathon hosted for teenagers by Hack Club, a nonprofit organization, had just recently ended. I had made many great projects, and I even got a 3D printer, completely for free, because of my work. I was locked and loaded to make another coding project, but I wasn't sure what program I should do it with. So, I stopped for a few days, and eventually found Pixl, something very like Stardance. In fact, they were so similar to each other that I was able to get right back into it and created Corpustein, a blazingly fast N-gram Markov Chain model with a configurable order and a rolling window system, in just 34 hours over 13 days. It is coded completely in the C++20 STL, and it provides an interactive and beautiful TUI just through a user-input loop and ANSI codes.

If you are very confused as to what Corpustein is, it is a mini AI model that generates text token by token using a window of previous tokens (or words) and a container of all the possible n-grams (or groups of X tokens) based on the current window. This is what an N-gram Markov chain (plus a rolling window system) is. It also maintains a set of previously generated tokens to prevent repeating them, but allows common English words to be repeated. Corpustein is also the TUI that lets users interface with it. The thing that makes it different from what you probably think of when you hear "Artificial Intelligence" (most likely a Large Language Model) is that a Markov chain does not remember anything larger than its N-gram window, but an LLM has an attention model, which looks at a very long sequence of tokens to help generate responses. And, with LLMs, semantic similarity is automatically encoded as high-dimensional coordinates in a continuous vector space, while Markov Chains rely on matching exact word sequences. LLMs can also generate reasonable answers to questions they've never seen before because of how they learn more abstract rules, logic, and world knowledge. Whereas Markov Chains usually just repeat fragments of their training data. An LLM is also much slower than a Markov Chain and is way more resource-intensive. Think of Corpustein as a statistical or probabilistic model that generates mostly coherent English.

In my previous project, MDEZ++, I didn't think I got enough experience with actual C++, without the Qt Framework simplifying everything for me. If you want to read the article about it, look here. I definitely can not say the same thing here. I think this was the best thing I've ever done for my low-level coding skills, ever.

Check out the GitHub repository here.

If you are a Hack Club member, you can access the project page here.

If you want a quick download, check this table!

Linux Windows macOS
Linux Executable tar.gz (x86_64) Windows Executable ZIP (x86_64) Not Automatically Compiled by CI/CD

Features

  • Fast and Lightweight: Built only on the C++20 STL, Corpustein is fast and consumes virtually no resources.
  • Custom Corpus Loading: Users can load custom corpus files to be used by Corpustein. Additionally, Corpustein comes with a vast array of default options already baked into the program for them to load.
  • Automatic Configuration: Corpus files contain metadata that provides default settings for the model to use, determined by the content of the corpus by its creator. If the file appears to just be a normal text file without any sort of metadata, it will skip the default settings gracefully.
  • Compatibility: With portable, native binaries automatically generated by the CI/CD for both Linux and Windows, Corpustein can be used on just about any system.
  • Commands and Settings: Corpustein contains various commands users can run while in the interactive terminal environment to control many things about the model, like the order, maximum sentence count, and much more.
  • Alternate Terminal Buffer: Corpustein uses an alternate terminal buffer to make a beautiful, stylized environment. Users are able to enable and disable this alternate terminal buffer right in the CLI.
  • Discrete Handling: When the model runs out of token choices, instead of simply stopping the answer, it will choose a new, random token to continue generating text, with the user never knowing it ran out of tokens in the first place.
  • Context-Intelligent Repetition Avoidance: Corpustein saves tokens to a history set to prevent repetition in its responses. It references tokens with a set of common English words to never force it into choosing a completely random token because of the avoidance of basic linguistic structural words
  • Configurable Typewriting Animation: Instead of throwing the model's entire response to the terminal all at once because of how fast it is, it uses a configurable typewriting animation to make it more appealing.

Devlogs

1: "Minimum Viable Product"

For the past 5.5 hours, I have been working on Corpustein. Corpustein is a Markov Chain built in C++20. I don't have a nice description or branding phrase yet, because I have been waiting for it actually to be slightly usable. Before I make my README, I will set up a GitHub Actions workflow to automatically compile Linux AppImage and Windows EXE files and attach them to Releases. How it works is that the user inputs a prompt, like "What is a transistor?" and the first step is finding a token for the program to start its response with. If you are wondering, a token is one unit of text. Usually, it is a word (that is, for Corpustein), but it could also be a character, punctuation mark, sentence, etc. It will compare the tokens in the user's prompt to the corpus to find a word the user said that is also in the corpus. And basic words like "in", "there", "a", "an", etc., can never be the seed. If it can't find a good seed based on the input text, it will just do a random one. It uses a rolling window where it stores three tokens at once, uses those tokens to find the best next token, and throws out the oldest token from the window so it's still only three tokens. Whenever it runs out of choices, it'll just go get a random window, continue, and everything will be okay. Currently, it has no way to know when to stop. That will be another thing I will do soon. It will just print text forever. The good thing is it doesn't repeat tokens, and it makes understandable sentences.

====================
corpustein v0.1.0
====================

User: What is a transistor?
Corpustein: the transistor in 1947, which significantly compacted computers and led the digital transition. Information technology, particularly optical fiber and main electronic components (resistors, capacitors, etc.) can be created at a microscopic level. Nanoelectronics is Forest in 1914"

2: "First Release, and Nice Styling!"

I just got the first release out, right here: https://github.com/tyleruploads/corpustein/releases/tag/v0.1.0. And it is precompiled for the user, which is pretty nice. That's from the GitHub Actions Workflow I just made. I also made it look a LOT better! I used an alternate terminal buffer to apply some cool styling.

3: "Added some Settings"

I just added many settings to Corpustein, along with some features too! The first feature is that now, text is streamed to the terminal with a custom typewrite() function. It streams it character by character, waiting a specific amount of time between each one. A setting was added to control the delay between each character. This next setting is probably the most important one, though. I made it so the user can configure the order of the n-gram model. The order is how many tokens it references to figure out the next token. These two settings were originally their own, but I decided to instead make a /set command and put them in there, as /set delay and /set order. I also made a subcommand in /set called max_sentence_count that allows the user to configure how many sentences the model is allowed to output per response. It also automatically scales the maximum tokens per response to 40 times the new sentences. This setting can not be raised higher than 50. Another important thing isthat I gave users the option to enable or disable the alternate buffer. That is pretty important, since if the alternate buffer is on, they can not do any scrolling, and everything is lost when the application is exited. Whereas, without the alternate terminal buffer, they can scroll and keep the responses after they exit the program. This can be accessed by the altbuffer subcommand in /set. Finally, I made it so anything starting with / but isn't a real command will just do the help command instead of outputting text.

4: "A lot of stuff"

Many changes have just been made. Most of these are really large architectural changes. So, here's an ORDERED BY SIGNIFICANCE numbered list.

  1. User-Defined and Multiple Default Corpus Support: Now, there are multiple default corpora, as opposed to just one. At the moment, there are 10, consisting of things such as the complete works of William Shakespeare, Mark Twain, and Charles Dickens, every single United States Presidential Inaugural Speech, the Linux Kernel Documentation, and more. Users can also load their own corpora by file path. This can be done with the command /load . Run /load help to view the types. The corpora start with a special format that starts off with a special file signature, then includes some default settings between the signature and the delimiter at the end (===). Here is how a heading looks: 
io.github.tyleruploads.corpustein:corpus-file
name: The name of the Corpus
default_order: An integer between 1 and 8 representing the order of the n-gram model
max_sentence_count: An integer representing the maximum sentences for each model's output, which also scales up the maximum tokens and the token history container.
===
  1. /stats command: A brand new /stats command has been added! It outputs the name of the current corpus, along with many other things such as the tokens in said corpus, the unique N-gram contexts that occurred as a result of the corpus and the order, and some variables not inherently associated with the corpus, like the maximum sentence count and more.
  2. Static Assertion and Preprocessor Directive Right at the Top: Right at the top of the code, a preprocessor directive and static assertion have been added (the static assertion is not in the preprocessor directive). The static assertion ensures it is being compiled with C++20 or higher. The preprocessor directive invokes an error when APP_VERSION is not defined, which prevents a big wall of fatal errors from being shown to the user with no context. APP_VERSION is automatically passed by CMake.

5: "Small but Large Stuff"

I just made some changes to Corpustein that appear small, but are actually large. I will list them here in the order of their commits, because I really don't feel like ordering them by significance again and finicking around with changing all the list numbers on my own when I move around points. The extra half hour is explained in the "Add Features Section to README" point.

  • Fixed Silent Error: The code has an unordered set named unordered_repeats that contains a bunch of common English words. The model is programmed to never repeat tokens that are in its token history window, which is equal to four tenths of the maximum token count, which is 40 times greater than the maximum sentence count. If it can not find a token that is not already in the token history after five retries, it will go to a random token. The purpose of the allowed_repeats unordered set is to make sure it is allowed to repeat basic linguistic constructs, such as "the", "and", "he", etc. After checking the code with clang-tidy, I noticed that some of the elements of the unordered set did not have commas after them, which linked some words together. For example, instead of two elements, "himself" and "herself", it was "himselfherself" (just an example; those specific words were not combined in the real program).
  • Add Windows Compilation to CI/CD: If you've seen some of my other coding projects, you know that this obviously wasn't done in one commit. It took me four to prevent errors caused by things like not specifying the C++ standard properly (that's what I thought it was when I made the commit, but that wasn't the issue), not using the POSIX version of MinGW, and using Ubuntu 22.04. The Ubuntu version was the main cause of all the errors. With Ubuntu 22.04, it comes with C++11. While it compiled the Linux version fine and used C++20, when I compiled for Windows with the MinGW toolchain, it used C++11 instead of C++20, which obviously didn't work for my application.
  • Update README Downloads Section: The downloads section of the README was a bit barren. So, I made a downloads table that now lists the Linux version, the Windows version, and the macOS version (or lack thereof). I also threw in a note for Linux users and for Windows users. The note for Linux users was essentially just: "Mark it as executable" (and some Bash commands in case they're really tired or something and can't do it on their own). But the note for Windows users was essentially just a full tutorial, because I had to include stuff about SmartScreen activation and stuff. And with Linux, I knew I didn't need to write that much, since it's self-evident they have some idea what to do with a tar.gz. The Bash command block was good enough. But for Windows users, I had to throw in the "What do I do with a ZIP File?" segment I derived from my previous project's README.
  • Add Features Section to README: This is self-explanatory. I just added some features to the README. But there was a really hard thing with it. Because I know all of my code so good, I couldn't think of anything special or worth nothing about my app. It was just the curse of knowledge. So, I physically printed out my code file and annotated it with my favorite pen (UniBall Signo 207, Black) and made markings like "Modular Design," "Robust Error Handling," "Advanced State Handling," "Fast and lightweight approach," "UX," "Windows UTF-8 Declaration," and a lot of other stuff. Most of it was just nonsense, like if I were a markov model designed to write corporate nonsense. But I eventually narrowed it down. This took about a half hour of manual pen and paper markings not counted by Hackatime, so I am manually adding one extra half hour for this journal entry.
  • Add Corpus File and Directory Structure Sections to README: Since Corpustein needs a specific directory structure and supports a custom corpus file format (still plaintext, designed by me, just for this app) to load default settings, I decided to make sure that's evident in the README.
  • Add Cornel Movie-Dialog Corpus: I usually don't put single corpora additions in these journal entries. But this one's pretty important, so I decided to. Fun fact: the corpus has 304,719 lines of text. That's a lot. And the really interesting thing is that it has 3,201,791 tokens in it, which makes 1,150,080 unique N-gram contexts with an order of 2. That means there were approximately 10.5 tokens per line. This corpus is definitely the most conversational.

6: "Analysis and Commands"

Those two words, analysis and commands, can summarize this devlog.

For analysis, I made cppcheck, clang-tidy, and (not technically analysis, but close enough), clang-format and address sanitizers automatically run every debug build. It makes the code much more readable, modern, fast, and less error-prone.

For Commands, I added /about, /reload and /history. I really don't need to explain those.

7: "Linux and Optimization"

From my last entry, I have made 6 commits (not counting bumping it to version v0.4.0). Almost all of these relate to either Linux or optimization.

  • Allow Linux Users to Store Default Corpora in /usr/local/share/corpustein/corpora: If you are reading that and think it's very peculiar, it'll make sense when you read a bit more. If you don't use Linux and have no clue what /usr/local/share is for, it's where applications store files.
  • Make Optimizations and Add Basic Profiling: The optimizations in this point simply consist of making the allowed_repeats unordered set a const reference in the arguments for the get_seed() function (which returns a string), making the tokens vector of strings in the get_ngram_contexts() arguments a const reference, and making another string a const reference. For profiling, I made a Timer class and used it to measure how long it takes to load corpora. I also made it so that when the lines of the corpus are being sent to the variable, it adds newlines where they should be.
  • Generate Cleaned Tokens Set at Corpus Loading: Previously, it would clean EVERY SINGLE TOKEN IN THE CORPUS, AFTER EACH AND EVERY PROMPT! That's terrible, since there can be millions of tokens, and they never change after the corpus has been loaded. I have no clue how much faster it made Corpustein, but it must've been a lot. It's probably a lot less resource-intensive now, too.
  • Create Linux Setup Script, and add to README: Like my previous project, I had a Linux Setup Script. I copied most of it, then changed a lot of it. The main difference is that Corpustein uses a normal binary and other files it accesses that the user doesn't provide via some sort of UI, but MDEZ++ is just one single AppImage without any files the user doesn't provide via some sort of UI. It took a long, long time. I also added the installation command to the CMakeLists.txt. And I added the script to the README, of course. I am claiming one extra hour because of all of the testing this took, that wasn't in the code editor! I ran the setup script at least 100 times, because it oftentimes didn't work. And, if you're wondering, it was spaced way more than 2 minutes apart between the times I ran the script and made the changes, so the time in between isn't counted. 1 hour is probably an understatement, considering it is 6:11 PM.
  • Add /history to README: I simply forgot earlier.

Look at the Linux Setup Script:

8: "Optimization, Modularization, and SIGINT User Directive"

This seems like a weird name, but I'm going with it anyway. On the topic of modularization, I just replaced the ngram_contexts map to hold unordered sets, as opposed to vectors, which greatly sped up the loading. On the topic of modularization, instead of just having one main.cpp, I now also have function_runner.inc and load_corpus.inc. Each holds exactly one lambda function, and they are put in main.cpp with #include statements. If you don't know what an include statement is, it essentially just copies and pastes an entire file right there before compiling. And I made it so that when users press Ctrl + C, instead of just exiting, it'll ask them if they really want to exit. Keep in mind, it still has the feature from before where, when you press Ctrl + C while it is generating text, it will just skip the typewriting animation effect and print it out all at once. And, it's now v0.6.0! I think I'll make it v1.0.0 in a bit, but after I ship it! Yes, that's right, I think it's about time to ship it already! I really can't think of anything else I could add, because it is already so advanced!

EXTRA: Note Sent to Reviewer:

Hello, reviewer! You're probably wondering why I wrote these journal entries like it's a blog article. I came from Stardance, where everything was one. I do recognize that these journals might not be public, and if they aren't, I'll just put them on DEV.to.

Conclusion

If you couldn't tell, this is definitely a long article, probably almost 2,000 words. When I participate in Hack Club events, I keep pushing myself to be a better coder. This was actually my first project in plain C++20 STL, and I learned a lot from it.

Corpustein is currently in the review queue, and I think it's going to go extremely well. On the topic of prizes, here are some things I'm probably going to get:

  • Minecraft
  • 3D Printing Filament Grant
  • Steam Game Grant
  • Soldering Iron
  • Random Desk Object from Organization

Check out the GitHub Repository here. If you are a Hack Club member, you can access the project page here.
