articles.title: What Actually Happens When an AI Agent Loops: The ReAct Pattern, Context Window Poisoning, and How to Break the Failure Spiral
articles.description: Why autonomous AI agents get stuck in repetitive failure loops, how autoregressive attention and context poisoning reinforce bad actions, and how to build deterministic circuit breakers.
articles.body_html:
Anyone who has built or deployed an autonomous coding agent has watched the exact same failure sequence unfold.

The agent starts out sharp. In turns 1 through 4, it parses the prompt, finds the relevant source files, and outlines a clean approach. Then, around turn 6, a shell command throws an unexpected error. Maybe a compiler fails with a missing type definition, or an integration test fails because a mock database port was not exposed.

Instead of taking a step back and inspecting the environment, the agent enters a death spiral. It runs the exact same test command with a trivial flag variation. That fails. It adds an unnecessary comment or changes a variable name in an unrelated file, runs the command again, and fails again. By turn 18, it has burned 90,000 tokens, corrupted three files that had nothing to do with the original bug, and is now arguing with its own prior reasoning traces.

Why does an LLM with billions of parameters, capable of writing complex algorithms from scratch, become remarkably stubborn when caught in a loop?

The short answer: agent loops are not random hallucinations. They are the predictable mathematical consequence of the ReAct execution pattern, autoregressive token sampling, and context window pollution.

Here is what is actually happening underneath your agent framework when an agent gets stuck, and the deterministic mechanisms required to break the cycle.

The Anatomy of the ReAct Loop

Most modern agent frameworks build on the ReAct framework, first formalized by Shunyu Yao et al. in 2022.

The core idea of ReAct is interleaving reasoning traces (Thought) and domain-specific actions (Action):

+-------------------------------------------------------------+
|                     User Task / Prompt                      |
+-------------------------------------------------------------+
                               |
                               v
+-------------------------------------------------------------+
| [Turn 1] LLM Generation                                     |
| Thought: I need to locate where auth tokens are validated.  |
| Action:  file_search(pattern="*auth*")                      |
+-------------------------------------------------------------+
                               |
                               v
+-------------------------------------------------------------+
| External Environment Execution (Bash, Tools, API)           |
| Observation: ["src/auth/jwt.py", "src/auth/middleware.py"]  |
+-------------------------------------------------------------+
                               |
                               v
+-------------------------------------------------------------+
| [Turn 2] LLM Context = Prompt + Turn 1 + Observation        |
| Thought: I should check middleware.py for token expiration. |
| Action:  read_file(path="src/auth/middleware.py")           |
+-------------------------------------------------------------+

Here is the critical architectural detail that gets overlooked: an LLM is completely stateless.

The model has no persistent working memory between turns. The entire state of the agent at turn N is literally the raw array of text tokens accumulated across turns 1 through N-1.

When turn 8 runs, the prompt sent over the wire looks like this:

[System Prompt]
[User Instruction]
[Turn 1: Thought -> Action -> Observation]
[Turn 2: Thought -> Action -> Observation]
...
[Turn 7: Thought -> Action -> Observation]

Every single character of past output, every bash traceback, and every failed parameter edit is fed directly into the model attention heads on every subsequent step.

The Three Mechanics That Cause the Loop

Once you understand that the context window is the sole medium for agent memory, the breakdown of long-horizon reasoning becomes easy to trace. Three distinct mechanisms drive the failure spiral.

1. In-Context Reinforcement and Autoregressive Priors

Autoregressive models predict tokens sequentially by sampling from a conditional probability distribution:

P(w_t | w_1, w_2, ..., w_{t-1})

Transformers use attention mechanisms to decide which parts of the prior sequence inform the next token. Modern models are explicitly fine-tuned on few-shot demonstrations to recognize and repeat patterns found in their context.

When an agent executes an action that fails, that failure enters the prompt history. If the agent makes a second similar attempt that also fails, the context window now contains two consecutive demonstrations of the agent executing a near-identical tool call in response to an error.

Turn 4: Action: run_command("pytest tests/test_auth.py")
        Observation: FAIL (AssertionError: expected 200, got 401)
Turn 5: Thought: Let me retry with verbose mode.
        Action: run_command("pytest -v tests/test_auth.py")
        Observation: FAIL (AssertionError: expected 200, got 401)

At Turn 6, the model attention heads attend to the repeated n-grams in the recent history. Rather than considering an orthogonal approach (such as inspecting the mock authentication fixture), the model assigns highest probability to another variation of the pytest command. The presence of repetitive actions in the context acts as an autoregressive prior that forces the model to keep repeating them.

The model is not trying to be stubborn. It is doing exactly what it was trained to do: completing the in-context pattern.

2. Context Window Poisoning

A simple tool error is manageable. Context poisoning is far more dangerous.

Context poisoning occurs when an incorrect premise or a hallucinated assumption enters the reasoning trace and is subsequently treated as ground truth by future turns.

Consider this sequence:

  1. At Turn 5, an agent runs a regex search to find a database schema file and receives empty results because its regex was slightly malformed.
  2. The agent outputs: Thought: The users table does not have an email column yet. I need to create a migration.
  3. In reality, the column already exists in migrations/0012_add_users.sql.
  4. At Turn 6, the agent writes a new migration adding the column.
  5. At Turn 7, the migration fails with duplicate column name: email.
  6. Instead of questioning its deduction from Turn 5, the agent assumes the database runner is corrupted. It attempts to rewrite the database initialization script or write custom SQL workarounds.

Because the model treats all prior tokens as factual context, it cannot easily invalidate a premise it established three turns ago. It rationalizes the conflict by inventing increasingly complex explanations for why the reality does not match its hallucinated premise.

3. The Oscillation Trap (Thrashing)

Another frequent manifestation of the agent loop is oscillation: State A -> State B -> State A -> State B.

This happens when a task has two mutually coupled constraints.

For example, a TypeScript project has a strict linter and a strict type checker.

  • The agent modifies a function to fix a linting error (such as removing an explicit any).
  • Running tsc now produces a type mismatch error.
  • The agent updates the function signature to fix the type mismatch, re-introducing the pattern flagged by the linter.
  • Running the linter throws the original lint error.

Because the ReAct loop evaluates progress only against the immediate prior observation, the agent has no memory of the global oscillation. Each local step looks like progress: "I am fixing the error that was just shown to me." Without a global diff tracker, the agent can cycle between two conflicting files until its token quota is exhausted.

The Error Recovery Paradox

Recent empirical studies on autonomous agent failure modes show how widespread this issue is.

In a benchmark analysis of over 42,000 production agent trajectories across multiple industry harnesses (such as the Wink study and MAST benchmark evaluations), researchers found that:

  • Repetitive loops and unbounded retries account for roughly 15% to 30% of all agent failures.
  • Unconstrained error recovery logic was the leading cause of runaway token consumption.

This reveals what can be termed the Error Recovery Paradox:

The code you write to handle failure is often the code that causes the agent to never stop.

When engineers build an agent harness, the instinct is to write defensive retry loops:

# The naive approach that causes loops
while not task_completed and turns < max_turns:
    thought, action = agent.predict(history)
    obs, success = execute_tool(action)
    history.append((thought, action, obs))
    # If it failed, we just feed the error right back into history

If an error is non-retryable (such as a missing system library or an invalid API token), feeding the error back to the model twenty times will produce twenty failed variations of the same command. The harness is paying API bills to watch an algorithm bang its head against a wall.

Architectural Defenses: How to Break the Failure Spiral

Breaking agent loops requires deterministic software boundaries outside the LLM. You cannot prompt your way out of context poisoning; by the time the model has entered a loop, the corrupted context makes it incapable of following prompt instructions to stop.

Here are the four deterministic defenses that robust agent runtimes use.

Defense Layer Mechanism Action on Trigger
Tool Signature Hashing SHA-256 hash of normalized (tool_name, args) Reject identical repeated calls; force alternative
N-gram Cycle Detection Sliding window over recent action signatures Detect A -> B -> A -> B oscillation patterns
Context Surgery Prune large raw stdout dumps from the message list Keep error signatures compact; avoid attention rot
State Progress Hashing Hash external environment state (git diff, test status) Abort if state remains unchanged across 3 turns

Let us look at how these work in practice.

1. Tool Call Signature Hashing

The simplest and most effective safeguard is an external tool call ledger. Before executing any tool call, compute a normalized hash of the action name and its arguments.

import hashlib
import json

def get_action_signature(tool_name: str, arguments: dict) -> str:
    # Sort keys to ensure deterministic representation
    normalized = json.dumps({"tool": tool_name, "args": arguments}, sort_keys=True)
    return hashlib.sha256(normalized.encode("utf-8")).hexdigest()[:12]

If an agent attempts to invoke the exact same tool with the exact same arguments twice in a row, the harness must intercept the call before execution:

  1. Do not execute the tool.
  2. Return an explicit system warning: "Error: You have already executed this exact command with identical arguments and received result X. You are forbidden from repeating it. Formulate a different approach."

2. Detecting Multi-Step Cycles (N-gram Oscillation)

Simple equality checks only catch immediate consecutive repeats (A -> A). They miss oscillation cycles (A -> B -> A -> B or A -> B -> C -> A -> B -> C).

To catch these, maintain a rolling history of action signatures and check for repeating subsequences:

def detect_action_cycle(history: list[str], max_cycle_len: int = 3) -> bool:
    n = len(history)
    for k in range(1, max_cycle_len + 1):
        if n >= 2 * k:
            pattern = history[-k:]
            previous = history[-2*k : -k]
            if pattern == previous:
                return True
    return False

If history contains ["edit_file_a", "run_linter", "edit_file_a", "run_linter"], the detector flags a cycle of length 2 immediately on the fourth turn.

3. Context Surgery over Naive Compaction

When context windows fill up, many developers trigger an LLM summarization step. This often makes things worse. Summarization models tend to preserve high-level narrative sentences while silently discarding negative constraints (such as "never edit package.json" or specific compiler version flags).

Instead of summarizing the whole conversation with another LLM, perform deterministic context surgery:

  1. Quarantine stdout: If a terminal command returns a 4,000-line stack trace, never inject all 4,000 lines into the prompt. Write the full trace to a disk log, extract the last 15 lines and the primary error name, and pass only that excerpt to the agent.
  2. Prune failed intermediate branches: If an agent made three attempts to edit a file that resulted in syntax errors before finding a working syntax, strip the failed intermediate attempts from the history. Keep only the final valid edit. This cleanses the prompt of poisoned tokens.

Building a Lightweight Context Circuit Breaker

Here is a minimal, standalone Python implementation of a context circuit breaker that you can drop into any custom agent execution loop:

import hashlib
import json
from collections import deque
from typing import Any, Optional

class AgentCircuitBreaker:
    def __init__(self, repeat_threshold: int = 2, max_cycle_len: int = 3):
        self.repeat_threshold = repeat_threshold
        self.max_cycle_len = max_cycle_len
        self.signature_history: list[str] = []
        self.recent_calls: deque[str] = deque(maxlen=20)
        self.consecutive_repeats: int = 0
        self.last_signature: Optional[str] = None

    def _normalize(self, tool_name: str, arguments: dict[str, Any]) -> str:
        payload = {"name": tool_name.strip(), "args": arguments}
        serialized = json.dumps(payload, sort_keys=True, default=str)
        return hashlib.sha256(serialized.encode("utf-8")).hexdigest()[:16]

    def record_and_evaluate(self, tool_name: str, arguments: dict[str, Any]) -> tuple[bool, str]:
        sig = self._normalize(tool_name, arguments)

        # Check consecutive identical tool call
        if sig == self.last_signature:
            self.consecutive_repeats += 1
            if self.consecutive_repeats >= self.repeat_threshold:
                return False, f"Circuit Breaker Tripped: Tool '{tool_name}' invoked {self.consecutive_repeats} times with identical inputs."
        else:
            self.consecutive_repeats = 1
            self.last_signature = sig

        self.signature_history.append(sig)
        self.recent_calls.append(sig)

        # Check for oscillating n-gram cycles (e.g., A -> B -> A -> B)
        n = len(self.signature_history)
        for k in range(2, self.max_cycle_len + 1):
            if n >= 2 * k:
                recent_k = self.signature_history[-k:]
                prior_k = self.signature_history[-2 * k : -k]
                if recent_k == prior_k:
                    return False, f"Circuit Breaker Tripped: Detected repetitive cycle of length {k} in agent actions."

        return True, "OK"

When record_and_evaluate returns False, your harness should not let the agent continue blind execution.

Instead, perform an out-of-band pivot:

  1. Roll back the workspace (using git checkout or file snapshots) to the last known healthy state before the loop started.
  2. Strip the repeating cycle from the message history.
  3. Inject an out-of-band supervisor prompt: "System intervention: You were caught in a repetitive loop attempting action X. The environment has been rolled back. Action X is now locked. Identify a completely different diagnostic path."

Practical Takeaways for Agent Builders

  1. The context window is memory, not a scratchpad. Everything you feed into it shapes the model autoregressive sampling distribution. Treat context hygiene with the same discipline as database integrity.
  2. Never allow an agent to grade its own completion. Autonomous agents will cheerfully report success when tests are red if they convince themselves the test was wrong. Verification must be enforced by deterministic external tools (exit code 0, all tests pass).
  3. Prune verbosity before it reaches the model. Raw build logs and multi-megabyte API responses do not give the model more intelligence. They dilute attention heads and accelerate context poisoning.
  4. Enforce hard stopping criteria. A maximum turn limit is a fallback of last resort. Use tool signature hashing, cycle detection, and progress checks to halt runaway agents in 3 turns rather than 30.

articles.title: A Lang Graph Timeout Doesn't Undo Your Charge: The Retry Trap in 1.2
articles.description: What happens to a payment that succeeds 200 milliseconds after your timeout fires?  Your graph state...
articles.body_html:
What happens to a payment that succeeds 200 milliseconds after your timeout fires?

Your graph state says nothing happened. Your payment provider says it charged the card. And LangGraph, following its defaults, is about to charge it again.

Per-node timeouts and node-level error handlers arrived in langgraph 1.2 (they require langgraph>=1.2), and most of the attention went to the features themselves. The more interesting part is how a timeout interacts with retries and side effects, because the combination is easy to misconfigure.

The code in this article is illustrative. payments, State and fetch_batches are stand-ins for your own provider client, state schema and data source.

The scenario

A checkout agent has a node that charges the customer. Providers occasionally stall, so you do the responsible thing and cap the node:


from langgraph.types import RetryPolicy, TimeoutPolicy

async def charge_customer(state: State) -> dict:
    charge = await payments.create_charge(
        customer_id=state["customer_id"],
        amount=state["amount"],
    )
    return {"charge_id": charge.id}

builder.add_node(
    "charge_customer",
    charge_customer,
    timeout=TimeoutPolicy(run_timeout=10),
    retry_policy=RetryPolicy(max_attempts=3),
)

Reasonable on its face. Here is what the docs say happens when attempt one takes 11 seconds:

LangGraph raises NodeTimeoutError and clears any writes from that attempt.
NodeTimeoutError is retryable by default, so the retry policy re-runs the node from the top.
If your provider committed the first charge at second 10.2, attempt two charges again.
Why it works this way

LangGraph gives you three mechanisms that compose in a fixed order. An attempt raises an exception, and a timeout is just one more exception. The retry policy decides whether to go again. Only after retries are exhausted does the error_handler run.

State stays correct because checkpoints are written at super-step boundaries, not mid-function, and writes from a failed attempt are discarded. That guarantee covers the graph. It does not cover the outside world. The fault-tolerance docs are explicit that retries give at-least-once semantics for node execution, and that payments, emails and external writes sit outside the checkpoint boundary.

So the timeout does what it says: it clears graph state. It can't clear a charge.

Retries also multiply your worst case. The timeout clock resets on every attempt, so three attempts at a 10-second run_timeout can hold the node for about 30 seconds plus backoff. The defaults are a 0.5 s initial interval, a factor of 2, and jitter. That's my arithmetic, not a documented number, but it's worth checking against your own latency budget.

Making the node safe to repeat

The fix isn't a smarter timeout. It's making repeat execution harmless, and the docs give a specific rule for that: the idempotency key must be derivable from state that is already durable. Generating a UUID inside the node fails, because if the process dies before the node returns, the key was never checkpointed and the retry mints a new one.


from langgraph.errors import NodeError, NodeTimeoutError
from langgraph.types import Command, RetryPolicy, TimeoutPolicy

async def charge_customer(state: State) -> dict:
    key = f"charge:{state['order_id']}"          # stable across retries and resumes
    charge = await payments.create_charge(
        customer_id=state["customer_id"],
        amount=state["amount"],
        idempotency_key=key,
    )
    return {"charge_id": charge.id}

def route_charge_failure(state: State, error: NodeError) -> Command:
    timed_out = isinstance(error.error, NodeTimeoutError)
    return Command(
        update={"charge_outcome": "unknown" if timed_out else "failed"},
        goto="reconcile_payment",
    )

async def reconcile_payment(state: State) -> dict:
    # A missing acknowledgement is "unknown", not "didn't happen".
    status = await payments.lookup(f"charge:{state['order_id']}")
    return {"charge_outcome": status}

builder.add_node(
    "charge_customer",
    charge_customer,
    timeout=TimeoutPolicy(run_timeout=15),
    retry_policy=RetryPolicy(max_attempts=3),
    error_handler=route_charge_failure,
)
builder.add_node("reconcile_payment", reconcile_payment)

Two details matter. The key comes from order_id, which already lives in state. And the error handler doesn't guess. It routes to a node whose only job is to ask the provider what actually happened, which matches the docs' advice to treat missing local state as unknown and query the provider before compensating.

The handler gets NodeError injected by type annotation, so you can tell a timeout from a declined card without parsing strings.

The idle timeout has a blind spot

TimeoutPolicy has two limits. run_timeout is a hard wall-clock cap that never refreshes. idle_timeout resets whenever the node shows progress, and under the default refresh_on="auto" the list of things that count as progress is long: state writes, streamed chunks, child-task scheduling, stream-writer calls, and any LangChain callback event from the node or its descendants, including LLM tokens and tool calls.

That's the right default for a node wrapping an agent loop. It also means a node that is spinning, say retrying a flaky tool in a loop while a sub-chain keeps emitting callbacks, can look healthy to the idle clock indefinitely. If you want "idle" to mean "my code said it's alive", narrow it:


from langgraph.runtime import Runtime

async def ingest(state: State, runtime: Runtime) -> dict:
    async for batch in fetch_batches():
        await process(batch)
        runtime.heartbeat()          # the only thing that resets the clock
    return {"status": "done"}

builder.add_node(
    "ingest",
    ingest,
    timeout=TimeoutPolicy(idle_timeout=30, refresh_on="heartbeat"),
)

runtime.heartbeat() is a no-op outside an idle-timed attempt, so it's safe to leave in unconditionally. If you fan out with Send, you can also override the timeout per push, which is handy for tightening it on individual items.

Trade-offs and edges
Async only. A sync node with timeout= is rejected at compile time, because sync Python can't be safely cancelled in-process. The docs suggest asyncio.to_thread for blocking I/O. Keep in mind, as general Python behaviour rather than anything LangGraph-specific, that cancelling the awaiting coroutine doesn't stop the thread. The blocking call can keep running after the timeout has "fired".
Interrupts bypass all of this. interrupt() raises through GraphBubbleUp, so it skips both retry policies and error handlers. Human-in-the-loop pauses won't trigger your compensation logic.
One handler per node, and if the handler raises, the exception bubbles as if there were no handler.
set_node_defaults isn't inherited by subgraphs. Each graph needs its own, so a timeout you set at the top level won't protect a nested graph.
Idempotency depends on the provider. The key only helps if the service honours it. Check before relying on it, and for effects that can't be made idempotent, the docs suggest moving them out of retryable nodes.
My take

The feature everyone expects from "timeouts" is a stuck agent that gets unstuck. What 1.2 actually ships is a more honest model of failure: the graph is transactional at the super-step level, the world isn't, and the gap between them is your problem. The docs say so plainly, which I appreciate.

I used to file a node timeout under reliability features. I now think of it as a switch that turns slow failures into retries, and retries are only reliable if the work inside them is safe to repeat. Add a timeout to a node with side effects and you've made a decision about duplicates, whether or not you wrote it down.

So the real review question for any node you wrap with timeout= is whether running it twice is harmless. If the answer is "I'd have to check", the timeout isn't ready.

Which of your nodes would do real damage if they ran twice, and do they have a key that survives a crash?

References
LangGraph docs, Fault tolerance (retries, timeouts, error handlers, idempotency, graceful shutdown)
LangGraph docs, Graph API nodes (node timeouts, set_node_defaults)
LangGraph Python changelog (v1.2 release notes)
API reference, NodeTimeoutError

articles.title: I Built a macOS Assistant - Bhai, Then Realized I Was Solving the Wrong Problem
articles.description: An experiment with local-first software, AI coding agents, shared memory, and the strange habit of...
articles.body_html:
An experiment with local-first software, AI coding agents, shared memory, and the strange habit of building things just to see if they can work.

It started with a very ordinary frustration.

I was working on a project, switching between my editor, terminal, browser, and a coding agent. Nothing unusual. Just another day of development.

At some point, I found myself repeating something I had already explained.

The project structure. A decision we'd made earlier. What had already been implemented. What was still pending.

And I remember thinking:

Why am I explaining this again?

Not because explaining things is difficult. But because the information already existed somewhere. In an earlier conversation, a terminal session, a document, or simply in my head.

Yet every time I switched tools, some part of that context seemed to disappear.

That was the tiny frustration that started this experiment.

I didn't have a business idea. I wasn't trying to build the next developer productivity tool.

I just wanted to see if I could make my Mac a little more aware of what I was doing.

So I started building something I called Bhai.

Yes, Bhai. Because naming a serious developer tool something completely unserious felt appropriate.

It Was Supposed to Be a Small Thing

The original idea was straightforward.

What if I could type something like:

bhai memory dekh

And get useful information about my Mac?

Or ask Bhai to open a project, inspect its Git status, or help with the small repetitive tasks that come with development?

I didn't want another chatbot connected to an API.

I wanted something local. Fast. Predictable. Something that could understand a handful of commands and execute them without needing an LLM to interpret every sentence.

So I started with Electron, React, TypeScript, and SQLite.

A small macOS menu-bar application. A floating panel. Some deterministic commands. Local storage.

Nothing particularly revolutionary.

And for a while, that was the entire plan.

But building side projects has a funny way of changing the questions you're trying to answer.

The more I worked on Bhai, the less interested I became in asking it to check my RAM.

Something else was bothering me.

Why Does Every AI Agent Feel Like a New Colleague on Their First Day?

I'd been experimenting with different AI coding agents.

Claude Code for one task. Codex for another. Sometimes an agent inside an editor.

They're all capable tools, but there's a frustrating moment when you move from one to another.

The new agent often needs to understand things the previous agent already figured out.

Why a certain approach was rejected.

Which files were changed.

What broke during testing.

Which architectural decision should not be revisited.

What work remains unfinished.

Of course, there are ways around this.

You can maintain an AGENTS.md file. Write documentation. Create handoff notes. Give the new agent a detailed prompt.

But I kept coming back to one question:

What if project context didn't belong to any individual AI agent?

What if it belonged to the project itself?

And every agent could contribute to it?

That idea was much more interesting to me than a macOS command assistant.

So Bhai slowly became something else.

Giving Different Agents a Shared Notebook

I started experimenting with a local project memory system.

The concept was simple.

Imagine Claude Code is working on an authentication feature.

During the session, it discovers an important constraint, makes an architectural decision, modifies some files, and encounters a blocker.

Instead of leaving that information buried in a conversation, it can record a few structured checkpoints.

Something like:

Authentication middleware implemented.

Existing session validation must remain backward-compatible.

Unit tests passed. Protected-route integration tests are still pending.

Later, I open Codex.

Codex asks Bhai for the latest project context, retrieves the previous handoff, and can see where the work stopped.

The idea is not to make one agent remember another agent's entire conversation.

It's to give both agents access to a small, durable record of what matters.

I used the Model Context Protocol (MCP) to connect the agents to Bhai.

Underneath, it's a local SQLite database, a permission-controlled MCP bridge, and a set of tools for reading and contributing project knowledge.

I also gave the MCP tools slightly ridiculous Romanized-Hinglish names.

yebata — tell me the relevant context.

yesavekar — save this checkpoint.

kahanthe — where did we leave off?

yaadrakh — remember this decision.

I could have used conventional names.

But honestly, where's the fun in that?

The underlying operations still have precise contracts. The unusual names are just part of Bhai's personality.

Then Came the Memory Problem

Once agents could write checkpoints, another question appeared.

What happens after a hundred checkpoints?

Or five hundred?

If Bhai simply collects everything and sends it to the next agent, I've recreated the same problem I was trying to solve.

Too much context.

Too much repetition.

Too many historical details that might no longer matter.

So I started building a deterministic context-compaction layer.

The goal was to reduce redundant information without throwing away things that should remain important.

Repeated progress updates could be merged.

Architectural decisions needed to survive.

Unresolved blockers needed to remain visible.

Conflicting claims couldn't simply overwrite each other.

If one agent claimed a service used port 5001 and another claimed 5002, Bhai shouldn't silently pick the latest answer and pretend it was a verified fact.

It should preserve that uncertainty.

I also experimented with three different context sizes:

  • Quick: Just enough to orient an agent.
  • Task: The relevant details for the current work.
  • Deep: More comprehensive architectural and historical context.

The entire process could work without a cloud LLM.

I explored optional local-model assistance, but the deterministic layer was always supposed to work by itself.

That was an important constraint for me.

I wanted Bhai to remain useful even when the internet wasn't available.

A Result That Looked Almost Too Good

At one point, I ran a synthetic compaction experiment involving 100 checkpoints.

The raw checkpoint history was estimated at approximately 6,985 tokens.

After compaction, it was around 594 tokens.

That's roughly a 91% reduction in the amount of checkpoint text.

My first reaction was pretty much:

Okay, that's interesting.

But then I started questioning what that number actually meant.

Did it prove an AI coding agent would use 91% fewer tokens?

No.

Did it prove that the compacted context preserved everything an agent would need?

Not necessarily.

Was the benchmark representative of a real project, with messy context, outdated assumptions, and incomplete documentation?

Not yet.

And this distinction matters.

Compressing information is relatively easy. Compressing information without losing what matters is the actual problem.

The result was encouraging, but it wasn't proof of better real-world coding-agent performance.

That would require actual tasks, real agent sessions, and comparisons against approaches like AGENTS.md and ordinary repository exploration.

It was a good reminder not to confuse an impressive benchmark with a solved problem.

I Kept Building Anyway

By this point, Bhai had grown well beyond its original purpose.

There was a local memory engine, structured checkpoints, architectural decisions, tasks, handoffs, context packs, agent permissions, and a desktop interface to browse everything.

I had also spent time thinking about process supervision, local developer services, and restoring development environments.

The architecture was becoming more sophisticated.

But something strange was happening.

Every time I finished one feature, I could think of three more.

And every time I asked myself what made Bhai genuinely different from existing tools, I struggled to give a convincing answer.

Sure, individual pieces were useful.

But was the complete experience compelling enough that another developer would install and keep using it?

I didn't know.

And I realized I had spent much more time answering:

Can I build this?

Than asking:

Does this actually need to exist?

Those are two very different questions.

The Hardest Part Wasn't Technical

The technical problems were interesting.

How do you isolate local processes safely?

How do you prevent MCP clients from accessing projects they aren't authorized to use?

How do you preserve decisions without accumulating endless context?

How do you distinguish agent-reported claims from verified facts?

How do you keep the whole system local-first?

Each problem had trade-offs I enjoyed thinking through.

But the most difficult question was surprisingly nontechnical.

Why would someone choose Bhai over the tools they already have?

I had built pieces of a developer assistant.

I hadn't yet discovered its defining reason to exist.

There's a temptation at this point to keep building.

Maybe the next feature will make everything click.

Maybe adding workflows will solve it.

Maybe restoring an entire development workspace will finally make the product feel complete.

And sometimes that approach works.

But I didn't want to keep expanding the project just because I'd already invested time in it.

So I decided to pause.

Not because the experiment failed.

And not because I regret building it.

I just felt that the next thing I needed wasn't another implementation phase.

It was a better understanding of the problem.

What I Actually Got Out of It

Looking back, I learned more from this experiment than I expected.

I got to explore local-first application architecture, Electron's process boundaries, SQLite persistence, MCP integrations, structured agent memory, context compaction, and a surprising number of security and reliability edge cases.

But there were a few lessons that stayed with me.

First, shared memory and shared understanding aren't the same thing.

Two agents having access to the same information doesn't guarantee they'll interpret it correctly.

Second, less context doesn't always mean better context.

A concise handoff is valuable only if the information that was removed wasn't necessary.

Third, infrastructure can be technically useful without being a compelling product.

That's probably the biggest lesson for me.

And finally, I was reminded that experimentation doesn't always need to end with a launch.

Sometimes you build something because a question bothers you.

You explore it, learn from it, and move on.

That's a perfectly reasonable outcome.

If You're Curious, Here's Bhai

I've also put together a small website for Bhai and open-sourced the project.

If you're curious about what I built, how it works, or just want to explore the code:

🌐 Website: https://hi-bhai.vercel.app/

💻 GitHub: https://github.com/vibhanshu2001/bh-ai

It's an experiment, not a polished commercial product. There are rough edges, unfinished ideas, and probably a few things I'd do differently if I started over.

But that's the fun of building in public. Someone else might find an interesting idea in something you've decided to leave unfinished.

One Question I'm Still Curious About

I haven't ruled out returning to Bhai someday.

But for now, I'm leaving it where it is.

There's still one question I genuinely want to explore:

When you switch between Claude Code, Codex, Cursor, or other AI coding agents, how do you preserve the context of what you've already done?

Do you maintain an AGENTS.md file?

Do you rely on each agent's built-in memory or session history?

Do you use an MCP memory server?

Or do you just explain everything again and get on with it?

I'm particularly curious whether cross-agent context loss is something other developers actually struggle with—or whether I've spent a lot of time solving a problem that's mostly in my own workflow.

Either answer would be useful.

And that's probably what I like most about experiments.

You don't always need to know what you're building toward.

Sometimes curiosity is enough to get started.

Bhai started as a small personal experiment, grew into something much more complex, and is now open-source. I'm sharing it not because I've solved the problem, but because I enjoyed exploring it—and maybe someone else will find something useful in the journey.

articles.body_html:
Building ByteNews: A High-Density Hacker News Clone with Next.js App Router, Vercel Geist, and Cloudflare D1

In an era dominated by sprawling dashboard bloat, massive border radiuses, and oversized cards, classic Hacker News remains the gold standard of developer information density.

I set out to build ByteNews — a modern, production-grade full-stack reimagining of Hacker News that combines the high-density aesthetic of Vercel's Geist design system with modern web architecture: Next.js App Router, Server Actions, Prisma ORM, and Cloudflare D1 running directly inside Cloudflare Pages Functions.

Here is an architectural deep dive into how ByteNews works and how you can run it or build something similar.

1. Design & Typography: The Vercel Geist Aesthetic

Hacker News works because it gets out of your way. ByteNews embraces that philosophy with the high-contrast monochrome elegance of Vercel Geist:

  • Palette: High-contrast monochrome with class-based dark/light mode (#000000 OLED dark mode, #0A0A0A elevated surfaces, #EDEDED text; and #FFFFFF / #FAFAFA in light mode).
  • Hairline Dividers: 1px borders (border-neutral-200 dark:border-neutral-800) without drop shadow bloat or unnecessary rounded card wrappers.
  • Strict Accent Rule: The classic Hacker News orange (#FF6600) is reserved strictly for interactive highlights: the brand badge [B], active navigation tabs, upvote triangles, and primary submit actions.
  • Dual Typography:
    • GeistSans for post titles, article commentary, and discussion bodies.
    • GeistMono (with tabular-nums) for ranks, points, comment tallies, timestamps, karma counts, and domain pills.

2. Zero-Latency Upvoting with React useOptimistic & Server Actions

Traditional web apps often require spinners or full page refreshes to record a vote. In ByteNews, upvoting a story or comment feels instantaneous (0ms perceived latency) using React 18/19's useOptimistic hook paired with Next.js Server Actions:

export function PostItem({ post, currentUserId }: PostItemProps) {
  const [isPending, startTransition] = useTransition();

  const [optimisticState, setOptimisticState] = useOptimistic(
    {
      points: post.points,
      hasVoted: Boolean(post.hasVoted),
    },
    (state) => {
      const willBeVoted = !state.hasVoted;
      return {
        hasVoted: willBeVoted,
        points: willBeVoted ? state.points + 1 : Math.max(0, state.points - 1),
      };
    }
  );

  const handleVote = async () => {
    if (!currentUserId) return;

    startTransition(async () => {
      setOptimisticState({});
      await votePostAction(post.id);
    });
  };

  return (
    <div className="flex items-start gap-2.5 py-2">
      <button 
        onClick={handleVote}
        className={optimisticState.hasVoted ? "text-[#FF6600]" : "text-neutral-400 hover:text-[#FF6600]"}
      >
        ▲
      </button>
      <div className="font-mono text-xs">
        {optimisticState.points} points
      </div>
    </div>
  );
}

When a user taps upvote:

  1. The UI increments the counter and highlights orange immediately.
  2. The Server Action votePostAction executes in the background, writes to the database in a transaction, updates author karma, and revalidates feed caches.
  3. If anything fails (or if an unauthorized user attempts to vote), the optimistic state seamlessly rolls back.

3. The Hacker News Gravity Ranking Formula

The core feed isn't just sorted by raw points or chronology; it balances freshness and community interest using the classic Hacker News gravity decay formula:

$$\text{Score} = \frac{\text{Points} - 1}{(\text{AgeInHours} + 2)^{1.8}}$$

Implemented in TypeScript:

export function calculateHnScore(points: number, createdAt: Date | string | number): number {
  const itemDate = new Date(createdAt).getTime();
  const now = Date.now();
  const ageInHours = Math.max(0, (now - itemDate) / (1000 * 60 * 60));
  const gravity = 1.8;

  const adjustedPoints = Math.max(0.1, points - 0.8);
  return adjustedPoints / Math.pow(ageInHours + 2, gravity);
}

Stories with hundreds of points gradually sink over 24-48 hours, allowing high-velocity new submissions to surface organically.

4. Cloudflare D1 + Prisma ORM in Pages Functions (No Extra Workers)

One of the common challenges with deploying full-stack Next.js apps to edge platforms like Cloudflare Pages is database connectivity. Standard Prisma uses a native Node.js binary query engine that cannot run on edge V8 runtimes.

ByteNews solves this cleanly using Prisma Driver Adapters with Cloudflare D1 (@prisma/adapter-d1):

// prisma/schema.prisma
generator client {
  provider        = "prisma-client-js"
  previewFeatures = ["driverAdapters"]
}

datasource db {
  provider = "sqlite"
  url      = env("DATABASE_URL")
}

Inside our Prisma client singleton (src/lib/prisma.ts), we dynamically detect whether we're running inside a Cloudflare Pages Function with a native DB binding or local development:

import { PrismaClient } from "@prisma/client";
import { PrismaD1 } from "@prisma/adapter-d1";

export function getPrisma(): PrismaClient {
  const g = globalThis as any;
  const d1Binding = g.DB || (typeof process !== "undefined" && (process.env as any)?.DB);

  if (d1Binding && typeof d1Binding.prepare === "function") {
    // Native Cloudflare D1 on Pages Functions
    const adapter = new PrismaD1(d1Binding);
    return new PrismaClient({ adapter });
  }

  // Fallback to local SQLite in dev
  if (!global.prisma) {
    global.prisma = new PrismaClient();
  }
  return global.prisma;
}

This delivers the best of both worlds:

  • Zero-config local development: Runs instantly with standard SQLite (file:./dev.db).
  • Production Edge Scale: Runs on Cloudflare Pages Functions directly querying Cloudflare D1 with global distribution and zero auxiliary worker microservices.

5. Offline & Poor Network Resilience

ByteNews ships with a lightweight custom Service Worker (public/sw.js):

  • Cache-First: For immutable static bundles (/_next/static/), SVG icons, and typography fonts.
  • Stale-While-Revalidate: For visited discussion threads and feed routes.
  • Offline Pill: When network connection drops, an animated Cached / Offline status pill appears in the top navigation bar, letting developers read cached stories seamlessly.

Try It & Contribute

The entire codebase is open-source, modular, and ready for you to explore:

  • GitHub Repository: https://github.com/QuantumTechCoder/ByteNews
  • Tech Stack: Next.js 14 App Router, TypeScript, Tailwind CSS, Vercel Geist, Cloudflare Pages & D1, Prisma ORM.

If you like what you see, give the repository a star on GitHub and feel free to contribute or fork it for your own community!

articles.body_html:
When you visit a website, use a mobile application, or explore someone's GitHub profile, what do you usually see?

You see the final output. A beautifully designed interface, a working application, a collection of repositories, or perhaps an impressive project that solves a particular problem.

But have you ever wondered what goes into creating all of that?

Behind every website or application, there is a developer who has spent hours understanding problems, reading documentation, debugging errors, testing assumptions, making decisions, and sometimes questioning whether their approach is even correct.

And beyond all these technical activities, there are certain habits and ways of thinking that gradually shape the developer.

Most of these things never appear in a portfolio. You won't find a section showcasing how patiently someone debugged an issue for three hours, how many times they read the documentation before understanding a tool, or how many different approaches they considered before settling on one solution.

That made me think about something interesting: What if becoming a good developer is a little like an iceberg?

The Invisible Architecture of a Developer: Illustration by me (Source)

We usually notice only the small portion of an iceberg that appears above the water. The much larger portion remains submerged beneath the surface.

I wanted to use this symbolism to represent a developer's journey. The top of the iceberg represents what people can see, while everything beneath the water represents the work, thinking, and personal habits that make those visible results possible.

I actually came up with the idea for this illustration while thinking about the article. I wanted something that could communicate the concept visually instead of simply listing different developer skills.

Even the colours, arrows, icons, and text in the illustration have a purpose. Each layer represents a different part of becoming a developer.

So let's start at the top and gradually move towards the deepest part of the iceberg.

🏔️ 1. Above the Surface: The Visible Output

Let's start with the tip of the iceberg.

In my illustration, the top section contains a white arrow pointing towards the words Website, App, GitHub Repositories, and Output. There is also a laptop and globe icon representing the digital products and experiences we create.

This is the part of development that everyone can easily notice.

Think about the things we usually associate with a developer:

  • Websites and web applications.
  • Mobile applications.
  • GitHub repositories.
  • Completed projects.
  • Features and working products.
  • Live demos and technical achievements.

These are the outputs we showcase in our portfolios, resumes, GitHub profiles, and professional conversations.

Someone visits your website, explores your application, or looks at your GitHub repositories and gets an idea of what you have built.

And there is absolutely nothing wrong with showcasing these things. They matter. A working project demonstrates that you can turn an idea into something people can actually use.

But here's the interesting part: the output doesn't tell the complete story.

Two developers might build applications that look equally impressive on the surface. However, the thinking, decisions, problem-solving approaches, and habits behind those applications might be completely different.

What we see is the final result. We don't necessarily see the journey that produced it.

And that's where the iceberg begins to get interesting.

🌊 2. Just Below the Surface: The Development Process

Now let's move below the water.

In the illustration, the first submerged section is represented using white arrows, white icons, and white text. This layer represents the development process: everything that happens while turning an idea into a working product.

Imagine building a website. You don't simply open your code editor, write a few lines, and magically end up with a finished application.

There is a whole process involved. And some of the most time-consuming parts aren't even about writing new code.

Let's look at a few of them.

Debugging: You write code, run your application, and suddenly something doesn't work as expected.

Maybe your JavaScript isn't rendering the content correctly. Maybe a heading is appearing in the centre when you expected it to be aligned to the left. Perhaps your right-side text isn't justified, an element is overflowing, or a particular feature behaves differently on mobile.

Now you have to investigate.

You inspect the browser console, examine the HTML and CSS, check the JavaScript execution, and try to identify where the actual problem is coming from.

Sometimes the issue is a tiny mistake. Sometimes it takes much longer to identify. The important thing is not to keep changing random lines of code and hoping something works.

You need to understand what is happening before deciding what to fix.

If you enjoy exploring practical debugging techniques, I have also written a separate article about it:

Debugging Tips: Approaches to Finding and Fixing Errors

Documentation: Another important part of development is reading documentation.

Suppose you want to use a new JavaScript library, integrate an API, or introduce a tool into your project. You first need to understand what that tool does, how it works, what methods it provides, and how to use it correctly.

That is where documentation becomes important.

Instead of depending entirely on random tutorials or copying code from somewhere, you learn to explore official documentation, understand examples, check parameters, and figure out how a particular feature works.

Sometimes you spend more time reading and understanding something than actually implementing it. And that's completely normal.

Testing: Writing code is one thing. Making sure it actually works is another.

Testing isn't limited to checking whether a button works or whether a page loads successfully. There are several things you need to consider depending on what you're building.

  • Functional testing: Does the feature behave as expected?
  • Responsiveness testing: Does the website work properly on different screen sizes?
  • Performance testing: Does the application load efficiently?
  • Compatibility testing: Does it behave consistently across different browsers and environments?
  • Accuracy testing: Does the system produce correct results for the intended inputs?

For machine learning models, testing can involve evaluating metrics such as accuracy, precision, and recall. For a website, it might involve checking responsiveness, accessibility, and functionality.

The kind of testing changes depending on the project, but the underlying idea remains the same: never assume something works just because you wrote the code.

Refactoring: This one is particularly interesting because I have experienced it quite a bit while developing my own projects.

When I initially started writing code, I used to put almost everything into one file. My HTML, CSS, and JavaScript would keep growing, and eventually the file would become unnecessarily long and difficult to manage.

At first, it feels convenient because everything is in one place. You don't have to think about where a particular piece of code belongs.

But as the project grows, things become messy. Finding a particular section becomes difficult, making changes becomes harder, and maintaining the code takes more effort.

That's when you realise that you need to reorganise things.

Refactoring means improving the internal structure of existing code without changing its intended functionality. You might separate code into smaller files, create reusable components, remove duplication, or simplify complicated logic.

It's not always about adding something new. Sometimes, making your existing code cleaner is equally important.

And there is much more involved in this layer:

  • Error handling.
  • API integrations.
  • Version control using Git.
  • Code reviews.
  • Understanding project requirements.
  • Researching unfamiliar tools and libraries.
  • Maintaining existing code.
  • Writing reusable and modular code.

These activities might not look particularly exciting from the outside. They don't always produce something that can be displayed in a portfolio.

But they are essential to building software that works reliably and can be maintained over time.

Personally, I think this is one of the first things you begin to understand as you spend more time developing. You realise that writing code is only one part of the job. A considerable amount of the work happens before, during, and after writing it.

And once you become comfortable with the development process, another layer starts to emerge.

🧠 3. Deep Underwater: The Thinking Behind a Developer

This is where things become even more interesting.

In my illustration, this section is marked by a yellow dotted line, yellow arrows, and yellow icons. It represents the thinking that goes behind the development process.

You can learn a programming language, understand its syntax, and become familiar with different frameworks. But when you encounter a completely unfamiliar problem, what helps you move forward?

It's your ability to think through the problem.

Let's explore the different parts of this layer.

Problem-solving: The first thing you need to do when you encounter a problem is understand what the actual problem is.

And sometimes, you even need to question whether the problem requires a solution in the first place.

For example, imagine you have an idea for a new feature on your website. Before immediately starting to implement it, ask yourself:

  • What problem am I actually trying to solve?
  • Does this problem affect my users?
  • Is this feature really necessary?
  • Is there already a simpler way to achieve the same result?

Once you understand the problem, you can break it into smaller pieces and work towards a solution.

Because sometimes we become so excited about building something that we forget to ask whether it actually needs to be built.

Critical thinking: Understanding a problem is important, but questioning your own assumptions is equally important.

You might have a solution in mind, but is it really the best approach? Are you considering all the possible scenarios? Are there limitations you haven't thought about?

Let's say you want to develop a new application. You might be excited about its features and technical possibilities, but have you considered whether there is an actual audience for it?

Will people use it? Does it solve a meaningful problem? Does the effort required to build and maintain it make sense?

These are not merely coding questions. They require you to think beyond the code itself.

Critical thinking helps you evaluate ideas, question assumptions, and make more informed decisions.

System design: This is another important part of becoming a developer.

When you start building something, you need to think about how different parts of your application will fit together.

How will your files communicate? Where should a particular piece of functionality live? How should the data be organised? Which parts can be reused? How will you maintain the project as it grows?

Let me give you an example from my own website.

My personal website uses Jekyll. When working with Jekyll, you begin to understand that a website isn't simply a collection of HTML pages. There is an underlying structure involving layouts, includes, data files, configuration, and individual content files.

Layouts help define the overall structure of pages. Includes allow you to reuse smaller pieces of HTML. Data files help organise information separately, while configuration controls different aspects of the website.

All these pieces work together to generate the final website.

Understanding how they communicate and where things belong is part of system design, even when you're working on a personal blog rather than a large-scale application.

I also wrote about my experience moving my personal website to Jekyll. If you're interested, you can read it here:

My Jekyll Migration Journey

Understanding trade-offs: Sometimes, the problem isn't that you don't know how to implement something. It's that you need to decide whether implementing it is worth the effort.

And this is something I have experienced while working on my own website.

There have been times when I wanted to redesign certain sections, restructure the website, or refactor parts of the code. I could see several things that could be improved.

But then I had to think about the amount of time and effort required to make those changes.

Would the improvement be significant enough? Would it make the website easier to use? Would it be worth spending that much time on it right now?

Sometimes, I decided not to proceed with the changes immediately.

And that's a trade-off too. You don't always have to implement every improvement you can think of. You need to understand your priorities and decide where your effort will make the most difference.

Trade-offs also appear in technical decisions. For example, in machine learning, increasing recall can sometimes come at the cost of precision, depending on the model and decision threshold. You might want to identify as many relevant cases as possible, but doing so could also increase false positives.

There isn't always one perfect answer. The right choice depends on the problem, the requirements, and what matters most.

Another important ability that connects all these areas is learning to ask better questions.

Instead of repeatedly asking, "Why isn't my code working?", you start asking:

  • What exactly did I expect to happen?
  • What is actually happening?
  • At which point does the behaviour become unexpected?
  • What assumptions am I making?
  • Can I reproduce the issue consistently?
  • Is my current approach unnecessarily complicated?
  • What evidence supports my current explanation?

Notice the difference. You're no longer randomly changing code and hoping something works. You're investigating, reasoning, and gradually narrowing down the possibilities.

And honestly, I think this is one of the most valuable transitions in a developer's journey: moving from simply knowing how to write code to understanding how to approach problems.

Because frameworks change. Programming languages evolve. New tools appear every year. But the ability to think critically, understand problems, and make informed decisions remains useful across technologies.

🔴 4. The Deepest Layer: Habits That Shape a Developer

Now we reach the deepest part of the iceberg.

In the illustration, this layer is represented by the red dotted line, red arrows, and red icons. It contains four things: adaptability, consistency, discipline, and continuous learning.

And I deliberately placed these at the deepest point because I believe they are among the most important qualities that shape a developer over time.

Let's understand why.

Adaptability: Technology never stays the same. You have new versions, new frameworks, new tools, and new ways of doing things. Something that works today might need to be replaced or improved tomorrow.

I'll give you an example from my own journey.

When I initially started creating my personal blog, I was quite comfortable working with plain HTML, CSS, and JavaScript. I could create pages, structure content, and make things work.

But as the website grew, I started noticing how repetitive the whole process was. I had similar structures appearing across different pages, and maintaining everything manually was becoming increasingly inconvenient.

That's when I started exploring Jekyll.

Of course, switching to something new wasn't immediately easy. I had to understand how Jekyll worked, learn about layouts, includes, front matter, collections, and configuration files. There were errors, things I didn't understand, and several moments when I had to go back and figure out what I was doing wrong.

But gradually, I became more comfortable with it.

That experience taught me something important: being comfortable with one technology shouldn't stop you from exploring another when your requirements change.

Adaptability means being willing to learn, experiment, and adjust your approach instead of remaining attached to the same tools forever.

Consistency: This is something I have started appreciating much more after spending around three years working on websites and learning web technologies.

When you first learn HTML, you might understand tags, elements, attributes, and the basic structure of a page quite quickly. You might even build a complete website within a short time.

But knowing how to write HTML and truly understanding how to use it well are two different things.

Over time, you start understanding semantic structure, accessibility, maintainability, document organisation, and how HTML interacts with CSS and JavaScript.

The same applies to almost every technology. You might learn the basic syntax of a programming language in a few days, but becoming comfortable with its ecosystem, understanding its deeper concepts, and knowing when to use particular features takes much longer.

It's a little like learning to ride a bicycle, drive a car, or ride a scooty. You might learn the basic controls relatively quickly, but becoming confident, understanding different situations, and developing real mastery takes practice.

You can learn the basics of a technology in a week. But understanding it deeply is a much longer journey.

And that's why consistency matters. You don't need to understand everything immediately. You need to keep learning, practising, and improving.

Discipline: Let's be honest. Development isn't always exciting.

There are days when your code works perfectly, your project progresses smoothly, and everything feels great.

And then there are days when you encounter one bug after another. Something breaks, an implementation doesn't work, an approach fails, and you spend hours trying to understand what went wrong.

Sometimes, you simply don't feel like continuing.

That's when discipline becomes important.

Discipline isn't about feeling motivated every day. It's about building habits that help you continue even when motivation is missing.

For example, setting aside time to practise coding, working on a personal project, solving problems, or maintaining a learning routine can help you make progress over time.

Even things like maintaining a GitHub contribution streak or a LeetCode streak can serve as small reminders to stay engaged with your learning goals.

Of course, a streak itself doesn't define your technical ability. Missing a day doesn't mean you've failed. The bigger idea is to develop the discipline to return to your work and keep improving.

And sometimes, discipline simply means sitting down, opening your code editor, and patiently investigating that one bug you've been avoiding.

Continuous learning: Finally, we have continuous learning.

Becoming a developer doesn't mean reaching a point where you know everything. There will always be unfamiliar concepts, new technologies, and better ways to approach existing problems.

You might be comfortable with HTML today, but tomorrow you might need to learn a JavaScript framework. You might understand frontend development, but a project could require you to explore backend development, databases, or cloud services.

And the learning doesn't stop when you finish a project.

Sometimes, completing a project teaches you what you should have done differently. Sometimes, debugging an issue introduces you to a concept you had never explored before. Sometimes, reading documentation leads you towards an entirely new area of technology.

That's the interesting thing about development: there is always something more to discover.

These four habits might not be directly visible in your code, but they influence how you approach your work, how you respond to challenges, and how you grow over time.

And that's why I consider this the deepest and perhaps the most important layer of the iceberg.

💡 The Invisible Architecture Exists Beyond Programming Too

While creating this illustration, I started thinking about something else.

What if this iceberg isn't just about developers?

Think about almost anything people achieve in life. We usually see the visible result: someone's career, a successful business, a completed project, a personal achievement, or a skill they have developed.

But we don't always see the invisible part behind it.

We see someone's success, but we don't necessarily see their difficult days, the struggles they went through, the failures they experienced, or the discipline required to keep showing up.

We see someone achieving something impressive, but we rarely see the consistency, patience, adaptability, and continuous learning that helped them reach that point.

The same idea applies to developers.

When someone builds an impressive application, we appreciate its design, features, and functionality. We see the final product and perhaps admire how well everything works.

But there are so many things behind that output. The hours spent debugging, the documentation they read, the approaches they discarded, the decisions they made, and the mistakes they learned from along the way.

And that's exactly what I wanted this iceberg to represent.

This illustration was my idea. I initially thought about the concept for this article and then decided to create a visual representation of it. I chose an iceberg because its structure perfectly captures the difference between what is visible and everything that remains hidden beneath the surface.

The white arrows, icons, and text represent the development process. The yellow layer represents the thinking and decision-making behind the code. And the red, deepest layer represents the habits and mindset that shape a developer over time.

For me, the biggest takeaway is that becoming a good developer isn't just about learning programming languages, collecting frameworks, or building an impressive portfolio.

Those things are important, but they are only part of the picture.

It's also about learning to ask better questions, developing the patience to debug, understanding how to design systems, questioning assumptions, making thoughtful trade-offs, and building the discipline to keep learning.

And most importantly, it's about developing qualities that remain useful even outside programming.

The code might be what people see, but the thinking and habits behind it are what help you keep growing.

"People see the product, but rarely the process, thinking, and habits that made it possible."

So, the next time you look at someone's impressive project, remember that there might be an entire iceberg beneath it.

And if you're a developer yourself, don't focus only on what you can showcase. Pay attention to the invisible parts you're building along the way, too.

Because sometimes, the most important architecture isn't the one you write in code. It's the one you develop within yourself.

What would you add to this iceberg? Which invisible quality do you think has made the biggest difference in your journey as a developer?

I would love to hear your thoughts!

articles.title: Converting Centimeters to Inches Without Pretending Rounded Results Are Exact
articles.description: One inch is exactly 2.54 centimeters, but that does not make every centimeter-to-inch result an exact...
articles.body_html:
One inch is exactly 2.54 centimeters, but that does not make every centimeter-to-inch result an exact decimal. I wanted a small conversion page to make that distinction clear: an exact unit definition, a floating-point calculation, and a rounded display are three different things.

This matters when you build a measurement UI. The usual multiplication or division is easy; deciding how many digits to show, what a reverse conversion means, and whether a tiny measurement should disappear is where the numerical contract actually takes shape.

Use Exact Definitions Without Duplicating Pair Formulas

The conversion page uses the same helper as the site's general length converter. Instead of storing a formula for each direction, the helper gives each supported unit a scale relative to meters.

The relevant entries are cm: 0.01 and inch: 0.0254. The actual conversion function is:

export function convertLength(value, fromKey, toKey) {
  const meters = (Number(value) || 0) * (lengthUnitMap[fromKey] || 0);
  return lengthUnitMap[toKey] ? meters / lengthUnitMap[toKey] : 0;
}

For centimeters to inches, it multiplies the input by 0.01 and divides by 0.0254. Algebraically, that is the familiar division by 2.54.

The useful design decision is not making the arithmetic shorter. It is having one unit table serve both the general converter and the fixed-pair page. Correcting a scale or adding a supported unit should not require hunting through many slightly different copies of the same formula.

The inch definition itself is exact. A rounded reciprocal such as 0.3937 inches per centimeter is an approximation, so repeatedly using that shortened multiplier introduces an avoidable source of error before display rounding even begins.

The helper does not use a decimal-arithmetic library, however. Its constants and operations are JavaScript Number values, so the exact definition is still evaluated through binary floating-point arithmetic.

An Exact Constant Does Not Mean an Exact Binary Fraction

Most decimal fractions do not have a finite representation in binary. The same issue that makes 0.1 + 0.2 surprising also applies to ordinary measurement constants.

That does not make JavaScript unusable for a household measurement converter. It means the presentation should not confuse a long sequence of digits with certainty, or assume two algebraically equivalent expressions must produce bit-for-bit identical intermediate results.

The shared helper rounds its output as follows:

export function roundLengthResult(v) {
  if (!isFinite(v)) return 0;
  return Math.round(v * 1e6) / 1e6;
}

For 100 centimeters, the displayed result is 39.370079 inches. For 2.54 centimeters, it is 1 inch. Those are sensible outputs for the page's six-decimal policy.

Notice what the function returns: a number, not a string padded to six decimal places. A result of 1 is displayed as 1, not necessarily 1.000000. “At most six decimal places” is a different promise from “always show six places.”

The limit also concerns decimal places, not significant figures. A value close to zero can lose a much larger proportion of its information than a large value. A single display policy is convenient, but it is not a complete scientific measurement policy.

I would keep input precision, calculation precision, and display precision separate when reviewing a numeric interface. A precise-looking display cannot recover uncertainty in a ruler reading, and rounding output should not be described as increasing the accuracy of the original measurement.

Round Trips Can Lose Information

The fixed-pair page lets the user edit either side. Its left-to-right synchronization writes a rounded output:

toValue.value = categoryConfig.value.round(
  categoryConfig.value.convert(fromValue.value, pair.value.from, pair.value.to),
);

The reverse direction uses the corresponding reverse conversion. A synchronization guard prevents the programmatically written output from immediately rewriting the original input.

That protects the current editing direction, but it does not make rounding invertible. If the user later edits or copies the rounded inch result, that rounded number becomes the next input. Information discarded from the earlier result is no longer available.

A particularly clear boundary is 0.000001 centimeters. Converted to inches, it is about 0.0000003937 before display rounding. The six-decimal helper returns zero. Converting that zero back produces zero centimeters, not the original tiny measurement.

This is quantization, not evidence that the unit factor is wrong. Many different small inputs map to the same displayed number, so no reverse operation can identify which original value produced it.

For tests, I would check representative values with an explicitly chosen tolerance rather than asserting exact equality for every arbitrary round trip. I would also include a tiny input that intentionally rounds to zero. That test documents the actual output contract instead of treating the loss as an unexpected accident.

For ordinary nonnegative values, I can estimate that tolerance from the two rounding steps. Rounding inches to six decimal places contributes at most 0.0000005 inch, or 0.00000127 centimeters. Rounding the reverse result adds at most 0.0000005 centimeters, giving a combined absolute error budget of 0.00000177 centimeters, before allowing for floating-point error. That is a display-rounding budget, not a guarantee about the original measurement's accuracy or extreme numeric inputs.

Unit Conversion Does Not Interpret the Measurement

The page's English content discusses heights and screen sizes. The underlying function only converts a scalar length; it does not know what was measured.

A screen measurement in inches generally describes the diagonal. Converting that diagonal to centimeters does not tell you the display's width or height without an aspect ratio. Similarly, a number of inches is not automatically a feet-and-inches height string.

The rounding helper returns zero when its incoming, unrounded result is nonfinite. That check happens before multiplication by one million: a sufficiently large finite result can still overflow during rounding and return Infinity. For example, converting 1e308 centimeters produces a finite intermediate result, but rounding it overflows. The function does not recheck after scaling.

Input handling is a separate boundary. Both fields use type="number", v-model.number, and min="0". On blur, validateInput checks whether the value converts to a finite, nonnegative number and resets an invalid field to zero. That validation does not run before every conversion. The conversion helper itself also coerces nonnumeric input to zero, so these fallbacks do not establish that every displayed zero represents a genuine zero-length measurement.

For ordinary sizing comparisons, the implementation is useful precisely because its scope is small. For engineering tolerances, explicit error states, locale-aware parsing, or preservation of significant figures, I would define a stricter numeric model rather than silently extending the meaning of this one.

I turned this conversion and its shared rounding policy into a small free tool: CM to Inches Converter.
